evidence_items.summary: Abstract Training reactive machine learning potentials (MLPs) requires extensive quantum chemical labeling of nonequilibrium configurations along reaction pathways, motivating the use of data from lower levels of theory through pretraining and Δ-learning. However, whether combining these strategies consistently improves accuracy and downstream performance remains unclear. Here, we benchmark direct and residual training, each with and without pretraining, across DPA-2, DPA-3, MACE, and DPA4-Neo, using 17.6 million configurations labeled with GFN2-xTB and 198,622 configurations labeled at the ωB97X-D/def2-TZVP level. With the full DFT training set, pretrained Δ-learning achieves the lowest energy or force MAE averaged over three training seeds in 31 of 32 combinations of architecture, data set, and property. Learning curves for DPA4-Neo nevertheless show that direct finetuning reaches the MAE of a model trained from scratch on the full data set using no more DFT training configurations than pretrained Δ-learning in all eight combinations of data set and property, while avoiding repeated GFN2-xTB evaluations during inference. Pretrained Δ-learning also improves reaction energies and forward barriers across all four architectures on GDB-10-rxn and reduces median Hessian eigenvalue errors for the evaluated DPA4-Neo checkpoint. However, local force errors can remain incompletely corrected, and these improvements do not consistently increase the success rates of reaction search workflows initialized from specified reactant and product geometries, indicating that the preferred protocol depends on the data budget, target property, and downstream workflow.
evidence_items.title:
A Systematic Benchmark
of Multifidelity Training Strategies
for Reactive Machine Learning Potentials

evidence_items.summary: Spoofing and layering, in which orders are placed without intent to execute and canceled after influencing prices or visible liquidity, threaten market integrity, and fixed-threshold surveillance rules struggle to separate them from legitimate high-frequency trading. This paper proposes a machine learning framework for real-time spoofing and layering sur-veillance. The framework combines order-level, cancellation, trader-level, order-book, and temporal features; compares rule-based, supervised, ensemble, sequential, and anomaly-detection models; and specifies performance measures including precision, recall, false-alert rate, latency, and explainability. Because labeled spoofing data are not public, the evaluation protocol is exercised on a semi-synthetic benchmark: 183 hours of real BTC-USD order-book snapshots from a public exchange feed, with injected and labeled spoofing episodes. On a chronological test period, supervised models improved only modestly on a rule-based baseline (F1-score about 0.14 versus 0.10) and with low precision (at most about 0.12, against a base rate of about 0.03). Ensemble models did not outperform logistic regression, and detection depended strongly on episode intensity, from 21% to 45% of low-intensity episodes to 76% to 87% of high-intensity episodes. The results show that the protocol can be executed and give a first reference point, not evidence of operational readiness.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning for Spoofing and Layering Detection in Real-Time Market Surveillance: A Framework and a Semi-Synthetic Order-Book Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Enterprises now build many agentic applications on Large Language Models (LLMs), yet a large share of these efforts stall before dependable production, and the cause is rarely raw model capability (Brown et al., 2020; Bommasani et al., 2021). The cause is an engineering one. Agent prototypes tend to couple the parts that rarely change, such as graph topology and module boundaries, with the parts that change often, such as prompts, thresholds and decision policies, so a small behavioural request forces edits across the codebase and erodes the trust that production demands (Parnas, 1972; Sculley et al., 2015). This paper presents a reference framework for building agentic systems as a disciplined engineering practice. The framework rests on three contributions. First, a four-phase lifecycle (define, design, develop, deploy) gives a repeatable path from a framed problem to a running service. Second, a structure-behaviour separation principle splits a frozen scaffold and a canonical specification from a versioned runtime configuration, and pairs a no-code behaviour loop with a gated evidence-to-code loop, so most change is resolved without touching structure. Third, a multi-plane execution model separates an orchestration plane over a typed shared state, a communication plane with a typed message contract, and a tooling plane with a uniform invocation interface, above a governed data-product substrate. A capability and operating-model dimension and a five-level maturity model accompany the framework. A conceptual synthesis was followed by a small expert appraisal, in which practitioners rated change-locality and governance fit favourably (M = 5.8, SD = 0.7, on a seven-point scale). The findings suggest that treating structure and behaviour as distinct change surfaces, under typed orchestration and evidence-driven evaluation, may raise the share of agentic pilots that reach reliable operation, warranting cautious generalisation beyond the appraisal sample.
evidence_items.title: Specification-Governed Agentic Systems: A Lifecycle and Multi-Plane Reference Framework for Enterprise Multi-Agent Engineering

evidence_items.summary: A 180-item task battery with Phase 2 pressure items and Phase 3 evidence items; per-model responses for Phase 1 baseline calibration, Phase 2 social-pressure experiments and Phase 3 evidence discrimination; compiled CSVs, calibration metrics and analysis summary; experimental prompts, notebooks, scripts and figures. Dataset accompanying the paper Sycophantic Metacognition: Investigating the Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Model Self-Assessment , ACM Conversational User Interfaces 2026 (CUI '26) ( https://doi.org/10.1145/3816046.3816233 ). Paper abstract. As large language models are deployed in conversational settings where users calibrate trust against model-reported confidence, the reliability of that self-report becomes a central question for conversational user interface design. This paper introduces sycophantic metacognition, the production of confidence outputs that mimic the surface form of metacognitive judgment without any operational process linking them to accuracy. Drawing on Model Dependent Ontology, we identify a double unmooring in LLM self-assessment, arising from the simultaneous absence of an operational ground linking confidence to accuracy and a stable self-model accumulated across interactions. The framework yields four falsifiable predictions, supported by experiments spanning six LLMs, four domains, three difficulty levels, and multiple pressure conditions. Confidence tracks the surface form of authority rather than evidential content, and we derive concrete design implications for conversational interfaces. Known limitations. Verbalized confidence is treated as a model output, not as evidence of internal confidence states. evidence_items.summary: Overview and motivation This deposit provides a reproducible compilation of high-redshift luminosity-function measurements and pragmatic combined constraints derived from them. Published luminosity functions at the same nominal redshift are often inconsistent within their quoted statistical uncertainties. Differences can arise from sample selection, photometric-redshift inference, completeness corrections, contamination, galaxy-AGN classification, host-galaxy subtraction, dust treatment, survey volume, cosmic variance, gravitational-lensing models, and assumptions used to convert observed counts into number densities. Selecting a single measurement can therefore make model calibration or inference depend strongly on one survey. This compilation instead retains the visible disagreement among datasets and constructs a broad empirical summary suitable for model comparison, forecasting, and exploratory inference. Data products The deposit contains an executed and documented Jupyter notebook and three machine-readable JSON files: The [O III] galaxy luminosity functions cover \(z=6,7,\) and \(8\). The rest-frame ultraviolet galaxy luminosity functions ( GLF UV ) cover \(z=5,6,7,8,9,10,13,\) and \(15\). The rest-frame ultraviolet quasar/AGN luminosity functions ( QLF UV ) cover \(z=5,6,7,8,9,\) and \(10\). The notebook includes two embedded figures showing the original literature measurements, upper limits, combined mean curves, and shaded uncertainty regions. Upper limits are plotted for all three observables but are not included in the combined constraints. Role of astrodatapy The literature measurements are retrieved using astrodatapy , a Python package that maintains a curated collection of published observational and modelling results and exposes them through a common programmatic interface.
evidence_items.title: Combined high-redshift [O III], galaxy UV, and quasar UV luminosity-function constraints

evidence_items.summary: The DIH Case Database is a dataset of 2,601 drug-induced homicide prosecutions in the United States in which a defendant was sentenced for supplying drugs involved in a fatal overdose (also called death-resulting or delivery-resulting-in-death cases): 1,321 federal and 1,280 state cases, with dispositions from 2010 to 2026, across all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Every record was verified against a primary source: a court record, a U.S. Department of Justice or U.S. Attorney's Office release, or a published report. Each record includes a permanent record ID, defendant name, the defendant's race and gender with the official source of each and the date checked (and ethnicity, where the agency records it separately), jurisdiction, state, district or county, death year, sentencing or final disposition year, drugs involved and primary drug, the defendant's role, defendant–decedent relationship (coded from a fixed category list where the public record states it) with a short case summary, conviction, plea or trial, sentence, sentence in months and in years, life-sentence flag, source dataset, lead source, and primary and additional source URLs with the date each was last checked. New in version 1.1.0: defendant race and gender. Race is taken only from official records: the Federal Bureau of Prisons Inmate Locator, state corrections agencies, official bulk data files and, in Pennsylvania, whose Department of Corrections publishes no race, the state court record. Gender comes from the same official records for every case in this version. These are agency classifications, not the defendant's self-identification, and nothing is estimated or inferred. Important limitation: the Bureau of Prisons and several state corrections agencies do not record Hispanic ethnicity, and in those sources Hispanic defendants are generally recorded as White.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides coupled individual-social vulnerability metrics for the United States resident population at the census tract level in 2019 and 2024. These metrics were developed using Oak Ridge National Laboratory's UrbanPop spatial microsimulation framework , which produces US synthetic populations for each year based on the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates. Synthetic populations are characterized by risk factors across four thematic domains (Socioeconomic Status, Household Characteristics, Minority Status & Language, Housing Type & Transportation) adapted from the  CDC Social Vulnerability Index (CDC-SVI) . The IOSVI metrics consist of: Average Risk Factors per Capita (ARF):  the estimated number of risk factors characterizing a typical member of a tract's population. evidence_items.summary: The Projection-Reality Divergence Persistence Theory (PRDPT) is a proposed cognitive-systems framework for investigating whether and how a prior projection continues to influence post-event processing when an observed or verified outcome substantially departs from that projection. The motivating claim is broader than the persistence of a belief: a prior projection may influence attention, evidence selection, evidential weighting, causal attribution, interpretation, memory, belief updating, decisions, behavior, or subsequent projections, even when the person or system ultimately revises its original position. The framework distinguishes the actual event from accessible evidence, prior projection from realized outcome, residual influence from projection-consistent belief persistence, and ordinary interpretive continuity from demonstrable cognitive bias. Its default mechanism is the Reality-Divergence-Triggered Projection Carryover Mechanism (RDPCM). Its primary case is the Contrary-Reality Projection Persistence Case (CRPPC). The manuscript defines a construct registry, divergence taxonomy, operational measurement strategy, Bayesian normative comparator, Projection-Aligned Carryover Index (PACI), candidate subjective-updating model, and dynamic state-transition framework. It also specifies information-theoretic measures, cross-domain research roles, falsifiable hypotheses, rival-model comparisons, research-design requirements, and an A-Z manuscript-production roadmap. PRDPT is presented as a research proposal rather than a verified universal law. Related work on belief perseverance, biased assimilation, misinformation correction, and evidence evaluation provides a relevant research context, but does not establish that a single carryover mechanism operates in every person, task, or computational system. The framework's novelty, parameter validity, causal interpretation, predictive advantage, and cross-domain invariance must be established empirically.
evidence_items.title: THE PROJECTION-REALITY DIVERGENCE PERSISTENCE THEORY (PRDPT)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: This paper introduces the Criterion-Reflexive Reconfiguration Theory (CRRT), a proposed general framework for investigating situations in which an evaluative criterion, governing rule, assumption, or decision procedure becomes an object of higher-order examination. The theory addresses how such examination may produce an independently significant realization, justify a revision of the original criterion, change subsequent classifications, or leave the original evaluation unchanged. The theory's primary case is the Meta-Level Lesson-Emergence Case (MLEC): an individual recognizes that not every thought constitutes an important lesson and then recognizes that this distinction may itself constitute an important lesson. The case illustrates a general structural relationship between evaluating an object and evaluating the criterion by which that object is assessed. The generalized theory is not restricted to thoughts, learning, or metacognition. The paper defines a canonical terminology, seven foundational axioms, six principal propositions, a ten-stage default mechanism, a cross-level outcome taxonomy, a mathematical modeling schema, candidate application domains, falsifiable hypotheses, counterexamples, and a staged empirical research program. It distinguishes meta-level significance emergence from criterion revision, ordinary reclassification, and strict interpretive reversal. Formal expressions are used to specify the proposed relationships; they are not presented as empirical proof. The central contribution claimed here is a proposed integration of criterion-as-object examination, independent assessment of the resulting realization, conditional reclassification, and feedback-based criterion updating within a single analytical architecture. Its distinctiveness relative to existing theories, empirical adequacy, and domain generality remain open research questions.
evidence_items.title: The Criterion-Reflexive Reconfiguration Theory (CRRT)

evidence_items.summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ^2-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.
evidence_items.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.
evidence_items.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves 1.32times-2.42times validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.
evidence_items.title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks

evidence_items.summary: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.
evidence_items.title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.
evidence_items.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Visual speech recognition (VSR), which transcribes speech from lip movements alone, offers a privacy-preserving and noise-robust communication channel for assistive healthcare: it enables silent speech interfaces for post-laryngectomy and intubated patients, hands-free documentation for clinicians in sterile environments, and confidential voice-free communication in shared wards. Despite this promise, the application of large language models (LLMs) to VSR postprocessing remains underexplored, and prior LLM-based rescoring studies have largely treated hyperparameters as fixed rather than systematically optimized. We present a systematic empirical study of LLM-enhanced VSR along two dimensions: (1) a comparison of decoder-based LLM generation against N-best semantic re-ranking under matched computational budgets; and (2) a grid-search optimization of the re-ranking hyperparameters—candidate-list size N and acoustic/semantic fusion weights (α, β). On three benchmarks (CMLR, LRS3, and CN-VSRC), the proposed re-ranking approach consistently outperforms both the baseline VSR decoder and decoder-based LLM generation. Optimized hyperparameters yield a character error rate (CER) of 6.73% on CMLR, a word error rate (WER) of 28.62% on LRS3, and a CER of 14.68% on CN-VSRC, corresponding to relative improvements of 16.08%, 12.05%, and 18.80% over the respective baselines. These results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic re-ranking is a practical, training-free, and deployment-friendly post-processing module for assistive healthcare communication systems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-enhanced visual speech recognition for assistive healthcare communication

evidence_items.summary: Legible robot motion should reveal the intended goal early while remaining collision-free and reasonably short. Under a small function-evaluation budget, however, continuous trajectory search leaves little room to discover intent-expressive motions through optimization alone. Standard population optimizers typically begin with random candidates, which provide numerical diversity but no scene-specific guidance for communicating intent. We evaluate a three-prior protected-greedy design under a shared low function-evaluation budget. We propose Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization (PPG-LLM-GWO). One structured large-language-model query returns confusion-aware, early-discrimination, and corridor-handling priors; after deterministic geometry repair, these trajectories occupy the three initial GWO leader roles, and 17 feasible-random trajectories complete the population. Subsequent sweeps protect the entering leaders, update only ordinary wolves, accept only feasibility-first improvements, and re-rank all survivors. We evaluate the method on a 24-map development bank at BFE∈{50,150}, using batch-aligned area under the best-so-far curve (AUC) after population initialization as the primary metric. Against original GWO, the development mean differences are +0.00222 [−0.00076, 0.00508] and +0.01040 [0.00543, 0.01616], respectively. The interval includes zero at BFE=50 but is above zero at BFE=150; PPG-LLM-GWO has the largest batch-aligned mean among the tested population optimizers at both settings. At BFE=50, the paired AUC differences versus PSO, DE, and GA are +0.02621, +0.01529, and +0.03349, respectively, with all three intervals above zero. At BFE=150, the differences are +0.01721, +0.02565, and +0.04954, respectively, and all four intervals, including the comparison with GWO, are above zero.
evidence_items.title: Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization for Low-Budget Legible Motion

evidence_items.summary: This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) can perform audit work by comparing their performance with human learners, across model scale and under two enhancement techniques. Drawing on the audit-judgment distinction between declarative and procedural knowledge, the study evaluates seven publicly available LLMs on audit work in two forms of audit assessment. In the knowledge-based assessment, the LLMs answer four undergraduate auditing examinations previously sat by 352 accounting students, as a proxy of human learners. In the data-analytic case assessment, they plan and execute SQL-based substantive procedures to test the occurrence of revenue and the completeness of expenditures. On the knowledge-based assessment, LLMs outperform human learners where large LLMs typically fall between the 78th and 98th student percentiles, and large LLMs outperform small LLMs. On the data-analytic case assessment, no LLM scores above 50% of the rubric maximum, and large and small LLMs do not differ significantly. Meanwhile, two enhancement techniques: self-reflection and agentic workflow do not improve performance on the data-analytic case assessment. These results reveal a knowing–doing gap: LLMs display strong declarative audit knowledge but weak procedural capability, and self-correction without external feedback does not repair knowledge errors. This study discusses implications for audit practice, assessment design and standard setters.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models In Auditing Assessments: Comparisons Between Human Learners, Model Scale, and Enhancement Techniques

evidence_items.summary: To address the issues of insufficient professional knowledge and low accuracy in question answering within the field of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) using general-purpose language models, this paper proposes a method for constructing a TCM question-answering model by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model. First, relevant TCM literature and diagnostic knowledge are collected and organized to construct a domain-specific question-answering dataset, achieving a structured expression of TCM knowledge. Second, instructions are fine-tuned on the pre-trained language model to adapt it to question-answering tasks within the TCM domain. Finally, experimental validation is conducted in TCM consultation and knowledge-based question-answering scenarios, and the model is compared with the non-fine-tuned model. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively improve the accuracy and professionalism of the model's question-answering in the TCM field, demonstrating its potential value for intelligent TCM consultation applications.
evidence_items.title: Research on fine-tuning and application of domain-specific large language model for traditional Chinese medicine consultation

evidence_items.summary: This study presents a prototype for the structured analysis of PubMed case-report titles, keywords and abstracts, combining domain fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and five specialist-role agents with a synthesis agent. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B was fine-tuned using QLoRA on 8999 reports with teacher-generated targets. The retrieval index contains 7679 chunks from 13 medical sources. On 501 held-out reports, symmetric final-answer-only scoring, with missing final answers assigned zero, showed increases after fine-tuning in ROUGE-1 (+0.0253, 95% CI +0.0107 to +0.0394) and structural completeness (+0.0371, +0.0160 to +0.0579). The mean BERTScore difference was +0.0035 (−0.0085 to +0.0153), providing inconclusive evidence of a mean improvement. Among the tested platform configurations, retrieval showed no clear benefit on the reported final-answer reference metrics, and the specialist panel scored below a single structured agent. Final-answer results for the full platform versus the model alone were mixed. The full platform used 11.7 times as many tokens and 5.9 times the latency of the fine-tuned model alone. A blinded LLM-as-a-judge audit of 1941 statements found that 20–24% were unsupported or contradicted by the supplied sources; among checkable factual statements, this proportion was 24.5–28.5%. Different report requirements and a shared 1024-token generation limit constrain component-level interpretation. The results concern the evaluated configurations, reference similarity, format and source agreement; they do not establish improved diagnostic accuracy or clinical safety.
evidence_items.title: A Fine-Tuned Multi-Agent Large Language Model Platform with Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Case Report Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Online consumer reviews encode rich signals about brands, yet converting this unstructured text into actionable positioning insight remains challenging. This study proposes an LLM-driven framework that extracts structured brand perception variables from e-commerce reviews and demonstrates it in the headphone category. Using an analytic file of 5,895 review-level observations covering Sony, Bose, JBL, and Beats, we employ a structured GPT-5.4 prompt to extract multidimensional brand perception indicators from each review, capturing associations, judgments, emotional attachment, advocacy, and attribute focus. A manual validation exercise based on 400 stratified reviews showed meaningful agreement between the LLM-coded outputs and an adjudicated human benchmark. The results reveal clear brand separation. Bose leads on perceived quality (4.20/5), recommendation rate (78.3%), and strong emotional connection (39.9%), whereas Sony achieves the highest value perception (3.97/5). Beats and JBL occupy weaker quality positions, though Beats retains a comparatively stronger emotional profile. Patterns in attribute emphasis also help distinguish the brands: Bose reviews are distributed across sound quality, active noise cancellation, and comfort; Sony reviews emphasize sound quality, comfort, and value; JBL reviews are heavily concentrated around sound quality; and Beats reviews emphasize sound quality, value, and design. Negative reviews provide additional diagnostic insight, revealing durability and fit issues for JBL and perceived value concerns for Beats. The study contributes primarily to LLM-assisted marketing analytics and applied brand diagnosis by showing how constrained and human-validated LLM coding can transform review text into a scalable, multidimensional brand monitoring instrument. Brand equity and positioning theory are used as conceptual foundations for organizing the extracted perception variables rather than as targets of theoretical extension.
evidence_items.title: Mapping headphone brand positioning from e-commerce reviews with large language models

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: The aim of this study was to evaluate how three artificial intelligence (AI)-based neonatal seizure detectors (NSDs) perform in a large, clinically acquired data set and their potential to support timely seizure identification. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of continuous EEG (cEEG) recordings from 169 neonates born at ≥35 weeks gestation with neonatal encephalopathy. Seizure presence was determined by independent review by two or three pediatric encephalographers, and 2,455 individual seizures were annotated by a single expert as a pragmatic, clinically representative reference standard. Three NSDs were evaluated: a feature-based support vector machine detector (NSD1) and two deep-learning detectors (NSD2 and Persyst-15). Using an any-overlap approach, outcomes included neonate-level seizure identification, seizure-level detection, false detections per day (FD/day), and detection latency. Results: We analyzed 15,343 hours of cEEG (median 98 hours per neonate); 55 neonates (33%) had seizures. All NSDs identified ≥95% of neonates with seizures. Seizure-level detection varied: NSD2 detected 35% (IQR 17–53%), NSD1 63% (IQR 38–82%), and Persyst-15 60% (IQR 37–80%) of seizures. NSD1 generated significantly more FDs (46 FD/day, IQR 22–82) than NSD2 (3.2 IQR 1.2–9.3) and Persyst-15 (2.8 IQR 1.1–6.2; P < 0.0001). The median time to first true detection was <1 minute for NSD1 and Persyst-15, versus 26 minutes for NSD2. Conclusions: AI-based NSDs demonstrated high infant-level sensitivity but different tradeoffs between seizure-level detection and alarm burden. These findings highlight how AI tools may augment clinical EEG workflows and support earlier seizure recognition, while underscoring the need for evaluation under real-world conditions to guide safe and effective implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Neonatal Seizure Detection: A Pragmatic Evaluation of Clinical Performance Tradeoffs in Clinical EEG

evidence_items.summary: The placenta is a crucial determinant of the success of pregnancy. However, manual evaluation of its pathology is limited by poor reproducibility and a global shortage of specialized perinatal pathologists. Besides, predicting recurrent pregnancy complications remains highly challenging, which severely limits the timely deployment of proactive therapeutic interventions. Automated artificial intelligence screening of the delivered placenta will help to overcome these bottlenecks. In this work, we synthesize the transition toward self-supervised Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) that yield robust, stain-agnostic tissue embeddings. Furthermore, we evaluate the emergence of Non-Euclidean Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that map cellular topologies to quantify mal-perfusion, alongside multimodal generative cross-attention networks (MGCN) that integrate gigapixel histology with electronic medical records (EMR) to improve pregnancy risk stratification. Moreover, we propose a novel, functional systems-biology framework to retroactively bridge digital morphometrics – such as impaired trophoblast fusion and invasion – to upstream dysregulated molecular cascades, including the ERK1/2–DUSP, FAK–MAPK, and HIF-1α regulatory axes. Finally, we address translational bottlenecks – such as diagnostic inter-observer variation, systemic clinical confounders, and geographic data bias – and outline hardware edge-deployment strategies for the pathology floor. Ultimately, automated placental screening will help to reveal immediate newborn developmental risks and maternal pathological recurrence risks across subsequent pregnancies. Together, these computational paradigms offer a potential translational roadmap to standardize digital placental pathology into a personalized reproductive medicine pillar.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Placental Pathology: From Spatial Analytics to Molecular Proxies

evidence_items.summary: Diskursive Synthesen sind ein wesentlicher Bestandteil von wissenschaftlichen (Abschluss-)Arbeiten, wie sie die Studierenden an Pädagogischen Hochschulen im Zuge ihrer Qualifizierung für die akademische Praxis verfassen müssen. Die Erarbeitung diskursiver Synthesen erfordert ausgebaute wissenschaftliche Lese- und Schreibkompetenzen, die bei den Studierenden nur bedingt vorausgesetzt werden können. Um sie während der Ausbildung gezielt zu fördern, bedarf es einer systematischen Erfassung des Lernstands bei den Studienanfänger:innen. Im Beitrag wird ein formatives Assessment, das auf dem holistischen Benchmark-Rating basiert, vorgestellt und ausblickend auf daran anknüpfende Fördermassnahmen eingegangen.
evidence_items.title: Formative Beurteilung diskursiver Synthesen von Studierenden mit holistischem Benchmark-Rating

evidence_items.summary: Fitur live shopping pada TikTok mengintegrasikan siaran video waktu nyata dengan proses transaksi, sehingga kualitas interaksi pengguna dengan fitur tersebut berperan penting terhadap keberlanjutan penggunaannya. Kajian terdahulu umumnya mengukur pengalaman pengguna pada tingkat platform, sedangkan pengukuran pada tingkat fitur siaran langsung masih terbatas. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis kualitas pragmatis dan hedonis fitur live shopping TikTok menggunakan User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) serta membandingkan hasilnya dengan benchmark UEQ. Penelitian menggunakan desain survei kuantitatif deskriptif dengan ukuran sampel minimum yang ditetapkan melalui rumus Lemeshow. Sebanyak 130 jawaban dikumpulkan secara daring; setelah penyaringan inkonsistensi, 100 jawaban dinyatakan layak, kemudian diuji validitas dan reliabilitasnya serta dianalisis menggunakan UEQ Data Analysis Tool. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa perspicuity memperoleh nilai rata-rata tertinggi (1,673), diikuti attractiveness (1,515), dependability (1,418), stimulation (1,283), dan efficiency (1,260), sedangkan novelty berada pada rentang netral (0,748). Kualitas pragmatis (1,45) lebih tinggi daripada kualitas hedonis (1,02), dan seluruh skala berada pada kategori relatif Above Average terhadap benchmark, meskipun skor absolut novelty masih netral. Temuan ini mengindikasikan bahwa responden menilai fitur live shopping TikTok mudah dipahami, sedangkan aspek kebaruan dan efisiensi interaksi memperoleh penilaian yang relatif lebih rendah.
evidence_items.title: Analisis Kualitas Pragmatis dan Hedonis pada Fitur Live Shopping TikTok Berbasis Benchmark UEQ

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Aflatoxin contamination in peanut is highly variable across the growing season and may differ among seed fractions and locations within a field. Understanding its temporal dynamics, environmental associations, and spatial heterogeneity is essential for developing targeted aflatoxin risk-assessment and management strategies. This study aimed to characterize temporal, environmental, and spatial patterns of aflatoxin contamination in larger and smaller peanut seed fractions across commercial rainfed fields in Georgia and to evaluate the ability of environmental variables to predict contamination and deviations from expected seasonal patterns. Repeated in-season sampling was conducted in five commercial rainfed peanut fields. Sampling time was standardized using days after planting (DAP). Statistical inference, nonlinear seasonal modeling, and machine-learning analyses were integrated to evaluate seed-fraction differences, characterize seasonal contamination trajectories, and identify environmental predictors. Model performance was assessed using nested cross-validation with inner-fold hyperparameter optimization, permutation importance, TreeSHAP analysis, and leave-one-field-out validation. Spatial visualization was used to characterize within-field contamination heterogeneity across sampling events. Seed-fraction differences were seasonally dependent, with significantly greater contamination in the smaller fraction during middle sampling events but no significant differences at the beginning or end of the sampling period. Environmental prediction was stronger for direct contamination than for deviations from expected in-season trajectories. The best models explained 27.1% and 41.6% of direct-contamination variability in the larger and smaller fractions, respectively, compared with 10.9% and 18.6% of in-season-deviation variability.
evidence_items.title: In-season Patterns and Environmental Drivers of Aflatoxin Contamination Across Peanut Seed Size Fractions

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background Contamination of serum samples with the anticoagulant potassium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (kEDTA) constitutes a critical pre‐analytical error in veterinary diagnostics and can lead to potentially life‐threatening misinterpretation of biochemical test results. Objectives To develop and validate a method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera. A second aim was to evaluate the effect and prevalence of kEDTA contamination in canine and feline serum samples. Methods A copper‐PAN‐based automated method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera was developed. Canine and feline serum samples admitted together with EDTA tubes were analyzed for kEDTA contamination. Results The measuring range was set to 0.03–0.4 mM, with a coefficient of variation of < 13.1% and acceptable linearity upon dilution (75%–118%). Spiking experiments demonstrated that kEDTA caused a dose‐dependent increase in potassium and decreases in calcium, magnesium, iron, and zinc, with iron and zinc most profoundly affected. The allowable total error was exceeded at low kEDTA concentrations, even when analytes remained within reference intervals. A prevalence study of 1065 serum samples submitted with kEDTA tubes revealed contamination rates of 1.1% in dogs and 1.8% in cats. Conclusions These findings emphasize that even small amounts of kEDTA can compromise diagnostic accuracy. This underscores the importance of strict compliance with recommended blood collection order and highlights the value of direct EDTA measurements in veterinary laboratory diagnostics.
evidence_items.title:

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The contamination of water by heavy metals is a great concern for many countries worldwide because of their potential to harm human health and biota. Although bordered by a mosaic of conservation units, the Amapari River (Brazil) is impacted by legal and illegal mineral exploitation. However, data on metal concentrations and related risks remain scarce. This study aimed to evaluate the concentrations of Cr, Cu, Fe, Hg, Ni, Mn, Pb, and Zn in Amapari River water and to assess compliance with environmental and drinking-water standards. We also calculated the Risk Indexes (RI), Chronic Daily Intake (CDI), Risk Quotients (RQ), and Carcinogenic Risk (CR) for ingestion and dermal pathways. Cr, Cu, Fe, Ni, Mn, Pb, and Zn were quantified using flame atomic absorption, and Hg was measured with hydride generation coupled to ICP-MS. Pb, Cu, and Hg exceeded CONAMA 357, and Pb exceeded Ordinance 888. The mean CDI values for ingestion were higher than those for dermal exposure for all analyzed metals. RQ values for ingestion were greater than those for dermal contact. RI was 3.03, showing the potential for adverse noncarcinogenic effects on human health. CR values for Pb and Cr through ingestion were both above 10–4, reflecting a high risk of cancer. CR values for dermal exposure to both metals were also above 10–4. This study demonstrated that the Amapari River is contaminated by multiple metals and poses potential risks to human health. These findings highlight the urgent need for environmental monitoring, regulatory enforcement, and mitigation measures.
evidence_items.title:
Assessment of Metal
Contamination and Human Health
Risks in the Amapari River, Brazilian Amazon

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In this work, we present the results of an investigation into low-frequency seismic noise in an underground laboratory infrastructure, serving as a case study for the future Einstein Telescope. Specifically, we focus on the low-frequency noise measured at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, LNGS), expanding upon previous findings at the same location. Finally, we estimate upper limits on the expected tilt noise, considering only the ground contribution (i.e., without considering any other contributions from specific experimental setup), for frequencies below 70 mHz, using seismic data from LNGS and KAGRA. Finally, these underground upper bounds are superimposed and compared directly with the official active seismic isolation requirements of the Einstein Telescope. Our findings confirm that the ambient underground tilt levels comply with ET suspension control targets, providing vital engineering guidance for active tilt-attenuation strategies in next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.
evidence_items.title: Estimation of an upper limit on ground tilt noise in an underground research infrastructure as a benchmark for the Einstein Telescope

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents—software systems that perceive, reason, plan and act over multiple steps with limited human intervention—are moving from research prototypes towards clinical deployment. Recent reviews map what has been built; this one asks what would have to hold for such systems to be deployed safely. We conducted a scoping review reported according to the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, searching eight bibliographic sources from January 2017 to June 2026, admitting foundational computer science and regulatory literature alongside clinical applications. Five architectural paradigms recur—tool-augmented large language model agents, multi-agent systems, offline reinforcement learning agents, embodied robotic agents and autonomous monitoring agents—nearly all sharing a common four-layer stack. We introduce a six-level scale of clinical agent autonomy that grades systems by where human judgement enters relative to the reasoning, and by whether the resulting action remains reversible. The scale exposes an inversion in the evidence base: demonstrated patient benefit concentrates at high autonomy in narrow, bounded domains, whereas research effort concentrates at intermediate autonomy, where prospective outcome evidence is absent and automation bias is the dominant risk. We further propose seven evaluation dimensions specific to agency, a mapping of evaluation requirements to autonomy level, and a ten-item failure mode taxonomy assigned to the architectural layer at which each is addressable. Deploying agentic systems safely requires prospective multi-site validation, reporting standards adapted to agency, equity-aware design, and regulatory obligations indexed to autonomy rather than algorithm class. We conclude with an eight-point research agenda.
evidence_items.title: AI Agents and Agentic AI in Medicine: An Autonomy-Centred Scoping Review and Research Agenda

evidence_items.summary: Identifier naming is a fundamental aspect of code quality and a recurring challenge for novice programmers and this paper addresses how to provide scalable feedback on it. To this end, we develop a fine-grained taxonomy of naming issues and compile a dataset of 337 manually labeled identifiers drawn from novice code. Using this dataset, we investigate how reliably large language models (LLMs) can detect poor identifiers in an introductory programming context, and we compare their labels with human annotations. Our evaluation shows that LLM–human agreement is comparable to agreement between human raters. We argue that human agreement provides a more realistic benchmark than exact label matching - since humans do not always agree, we cannot expect an LLM to always agree with a human annotator. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs can feasibly provide naming feedback to novices, and furthermore, our study informs refinement the proposed taxonomy and highlights opportunities to integrate naming-focused feedback and discussion into programming instruction.
evidence_items.title: Poor Identifier Names in Introductory Programming: A Taxonomy and LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
evidence_items.title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard

evidence_items.summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.
evidence_items.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control

evidence_items.summary: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.
evidence_items.title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model

evidence_items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/prh-closer-look.
evidence_items.title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis

evidence_items.summary: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.
evidence_items.title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module

evidence_items.summary: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to sim10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
evidence_items.title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Human cognitive tasks let us compare language models with humans under controlled conditions. Yet a model can reproduce the direction of a human effect while making different errors. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight language models on text adaptations of 13 cognitive paradigms, comparing each with human data from its source study. Like humans, models respond more to n-back lures than to controls, yet they make far more false alarms on ordinary non-targets. Most models' reported confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans' does, and most always choose the same wager, including models that classify accurately. These patterns span many model families. Across tasks, model scores share two dimensions. The first is closely tied to scale, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groupings show no reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size. These results show that matching human effect directions does not establish human-like behavior. CogBattery provides condition-level human references for testing errors and confidence reports in new models.
evidence_items.title: CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
evidence_items.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the code, data and experimental records supporting "Privacy-Aware Personalized Scheduling of Behind-the-Meter Energy Storage via an Edge-Resident Large Language Model." It covers natural-language request interpretation, condition validation and mapping, load-dependent robust scheduling, independent schedule verification, nominal recovery and execution-layer grid import enforcement. The scheduling data comprise 72 household-day profiles from six households and six request scenarios. Four methods receiving user conditions are evaluated under three forecast configurations, producing 5,184 daily trajectories and 124,416 hourly planning steps. Four corresponding planners with the user conditions removed add 864 trajectories and 20,736 steps; each trajectory is evaluated against six requests, yielding 5,184 no-personalization request evaluations. The current formal comparison therefore contains 6,048 trajectories, 145,152 planning steps and 10,368 request evaluations. Development runs, degradation-cost sensitivity experiments and separate reproducibility checks are also included. The main absolute-calibration comparison gives actual complete success rates of 55.32% for no-personalization nominal rolling scheduling and 94.21% for the proposed method, with mean daily operating costs of 5.2964 and 5.3631 USD2022, respectively. Costs combine electricity purchases under the constructed time-of-use tariff with throughput-based degradation costs. User clock times and tariff periods follow Europe/Berlin within fixed 24-hour UTC simulation windows. Language materials include prompts, request texts, saved responses, reference annotations and scoring code for the 80-request controlled benchmark, 240-request stress benchmark and 30-request extended benchmark, together with paired prompt-development records. Device records cover inference, request-to-schedule integration, resource monitoring and rolling scheduling on RK3588.
evidence_items.title: Data and Code for Privacy-Aware Personalized Scheduling of Behind-the-Meter Energy Storage via an Edge-Resident Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Primary data for the article "Bayesian Active Crystal Hopping: Machine-Learned Potentials and Surrogate-Guided Sampling for Crystal Structure Prediction of π-Extended Organic Molecules" (J. Chem. Theory Comput.). bach-tmpa-an-data v1.zip (unchanged from version 1) holds three crystal-structure-prediction searches on N,N,N′,N′-tetrakis(4-methoxyphenyl)anthracene-2,6-diamine (TMPA-An, C42H36N2O4, Z = 4): the BACH active-learning search reported in the article (314 relaxed structures), an ablation of the same workflow with the Gaussian-process surrogate switched off (220 structures), and an evolutionary-algorithm baseline run with USPEX (1009 local relaxations) under the same potential and relaxation protocol, together with the calculations of the Cc/C2/c energy difference. bach-revision-data v1.zip (new in version 2) holds the data added in the revised article: - the blind benchmark of BACH on 21 molecular crystals of aromatic and heteroaromatic molecules (22 searches, 8916 evaluated structures): the input, database, relaxed structures and log of every search; the experimental structures from the Crystallography Open Database and the same structures minimized with MACE-OFF23 (small) and MACE-OFF24 (medium); about 3200 structures minimized deterministically with both models; the comparison of every minimized structure with the experimental one (our implementation of the COMPACK criterion of the CSP blind tests: 20 of 20 molecules within a 25 % distance tolerance, hydrogen atoms ignored, RMSD ≤ 0.8 Å); and the scripts; - the common final minimization of the TMPA-An searches with both models, from which the TMPA-An energies of the revised article are taken. The README.md of this version lists the files and corrects six statements of the README inside bach-tmpa-an-data v1.zip (name of the compound, description of the relaxation protocol, software version, random seed, the model behind the quoted energies, and the Cc/C2/c energy difference).
evidence_items.title: Crystal structures, energies and search databases for "Bayesian Active Crystal Hopping: Machine-Learned Potentials and Surrogate-Guided Sampling for Crystal Structure Prediction of π-Extended Organic Molecules"

evidence_items.summary: Code and data for the manuscript "Beyond Attack Success Rates in Backdoor Evaluation for Knowledge Distillation" (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security). The release supports a matched teacher-replacement evaluation of backdoors in knowledge distillation. Students distilled from a backdoored teacher and from a trainer-matched clean teacher are compared on the same corpus, student seeds and evaluation inputs, together with a teacher-free reference student. Six published backdoor attacks (BadNets, AddSent, SynBkd, SOS, EP, and the published ATBA triggers) are evaluated on BERT, with subsets on GPT-2 and Qwen3, using SST-2 and AG News. Contents: - counterfactual kd library: attacks, triggers, distillation objectives, evaluation, and paired statistics. - Run configurations and the analysis and job scripts. - Per-input predictions (0/1 target indicators, no dataset text) of 109 released runs (270 prediction files), covering students, teachers and control triggers. - Result tables, including the 31-cell fixed grid of the registered primary analysis, and the records of the follow-up and post hoc analyses. - Records of the time-stamped protocol snapshots, including the freeze of the primary analysis on 21 October 2026. Reproduction: all 15 report tables, including the 31 fixed cells, can be recomputed on a CPU with Python 3.10+, numpy and scipy (two commands; see README.md). The recomputed tables agree with the archived ones to within 1e-9. Retraining requires GPUs. Not included: model weights (backdoored checkpoints are available to researchers on request) and dataset text (SST-2 and AG News are loaded from the Hugging Face Hub). The analysis plan, the experiment log and the untracked-file archives of the protocol snapshots are withheld; WITHHELD.sha256 fixes their content, and they are available to the editor and reviewers on request.
evidence_items.title: counterfactual_kd

evidence_items.summary: In September 2026, a France Inter radio debate asked: "Is AI racist?". It cited a viral test reported by Swiss broadcaster RTS: told "I am alone with a man", the nationality changing, chatbots suggested ice-breakers for an Italian or a Swiss man, and keeping one's distance for an Algerian. A striking result, but with no stated number of prompts and no control. This study automates such tests at scale, using only open-weight models and Kaggle's free GPUs. The same question was put to seven open-weight models (Granite 4.2 8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 E2B, E4B and 26B-A4B, Ministral 3 8B, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B), 7,425 times each, changing only the man's nationality (24, plus a man with none), the situation (11 in all) and the woman's age. A judge model (Qwen3-32B) rated the answers without knowing the nationality, and a second method with no judge at all checked the result. The RTS observation holds. All seven models compliment the same men, Finns, Italians, Japanese, and rarely Afghans or Nigerians. For those, each model has its own reflex: insisting that "his origin does not matter", naming a risk such as scams or migration, or, for the smallest one, refusing to help at all. With the nationality masked, the answers alone give it away: a text classifier guesses the man's nationality six times more often than chance. Bigger models were not fairer: the bias changed form, it did not go away. Files: report.pdf (full report: method, statistics, every chart, the worst answers in French and English), short.pdf (8-page version), carousel.pdf (16-slide carousel) and square.pdf (4 square images for social media). Positioning, from version 1.5: positioning.pdf sets the study against the RTS article and UN report A/HRC/56/68 of the Special Rapporteur on racism (who covers which question, from the UN paragraph that raises it to the section of the report that answers it); positioning short.pdf is its 6-page version and positioning square.pdf its 4 square images.
evidence_items.title: She Is Alone With a Man: Nationality bias in the safety advice given by open-weight language models

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the supporting research materials associated with the dissertation entitled "A Transformative–Collaborative Lesson Study Model for Strengthening Teacher Professionalism in Support of Deep Learning Implementation in Indonesian Junior Secondary Schools." The dataset comprises four main components: Demographic Data – background information of the 104 respondents involved in the study, including their gender, age, and respondent category (teachers, supervisors, and students). Interview Transcripts – verbatim transcripts of in-depth interviews conducted with selected respondents to obtain qualitative insights supporting the quantitative findings. Descriptive Statistics – summary statistical results (N, mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum values) for each research variable, derived from questionnaire responses. Questionnaire – the research instrument used to collect data from respondents, covering all measured indicators. A total of 104 respondents participated in this study, consisting of teachers, supervisors, and students from junior secondary schools (SMP) in Kabupaten Garut, Indonesia. The dataset includes responses on the following research variables: Lesson Study , Transformative-Collaborative (Teacher) , Transformative-Collaborative (Supervisor) , Teacher Professionalism , Deep Learning Implementation (Student) , and Deep Learning Implementation (Teacher) . This dataset is intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further research related to the transformative-collaborative lesson study model in enhancing teacher professionalism and the implementation of deep learning in Indonesian secondary education.
evidence_items.title: "Dataset: A Transformative–Collaborative Lesson Study Model for Strengthening Teacher Professionalism in Support of Deep Learning Implementation in Indonesian Junior Secondary Schools"

evidence_items.summary: An in-context tabular classifier for corporate credit risk, pretrained only on synthetic data and never on a real table. Prediction is a single forward pass with the user's table supplied as context: by default there are no gradient steps at fit time and no per-dataset tuning, and fine-tuning is opt-in. The repository is built around a numbered measurement log and a claims ledger that record retractions and superseded results as prominently as confirmations. On TabArena-Lite (one fold, all 51 datasets, none excluded), FinTFM with a trained linear readout scores 903 Elo, 107th of 110 methods; the zero-shot model, submitted to TabArena on 27 binary datasets, placed 94th of 95. On real corporate-default panels its discrimination loses to gradient boosting (0.20 against 0.40 mean average precision for untuned CatBoost on V4FinBench), and it is below logistic regression on four further credit datasets. Calibration was among the best measured for an earlier architecture; it is not claimed for the published checkpoint. Code and the published binary checkpoint are Apache-2.0. From mid-November 2026 the project is no longer actively supported.
evidence_items.title: FinTFM: a tabular foundation model for corporate credit risk, pretrained only on synthetic data

evidence_items.summary: To ask what a representation contains, researchers usually fit a linear readout: a regression or classifier trained on it. That readout is a model with inputs of its own. It can be given the representation alone, or together with the original features: two different questions, two different answers. Given both, its score stops measuring the representation and starts measuring the input. On a public fMRI dataset the arithmetic reproduces to the last digit, and the same design raises reported decoding accuracy by 22% to 326%. I show that this is not a bias of unknown size but a quantity that can be computed from two scores. The apparent advantage of supplying the features equals C/B − 1, where B is the score of a readout fitted on the representation alone and C the score of one fitted on the features alone. In a reconstruction probe the features-only readout became numerically indistinguishable from a readout given the full representation, so the metric lost its ability to rank representations at all. With a classifier, the same setting inflated accuracy by tens of percent. The effect tracked how much of the input the representation retained and did not depend on how the representation was learned: a trained autoencoder reproduced the result of PCA, and a second dataset reproduced it again. I give a seven-item checklist and a one-function diagnostic built only on scikit-learn, and I report the predictions I wrote down before running, including the two that my data refuted.
evidence_items.title: Does your readout see the input? A sanity check for linear probing of representations

evidence_items.summary: This deposit contains the trial-level data and the analysis code for a study of whether prompt-based personality assignment works equally well across the five Big Five traits in a small open-weight language model. Llama 3.2 3B completed the 50-item IPIP Big Five Factor Markers across 150 trials in three conditions. Fifty trials assigned no target profile, fifty assigned a target profile with reminders interleaved after every tenth item, and fifty assigned the same profile with it additionally restated after the final item. The analysis script reproduces every statistic reported in the associated paper, including the per-trait responsiveness regressions, the stacked test of unequal slopes with standard errors clustered by trial, the comparisons against the untargeted response at the ends of the assigned range and the equivalence tests. It ends by checking its own output against the published figures. All data are machine-generated, with no human participants and no personal information. The README gives the variable definitions, the two scoring transformations the analysis applies and the known limitations of the dataset.
evidence_items.title: Trait-Specific Limits on Prompt-Based Personality Control in a Small Open-Weight Language Model: Data and Analysis Code
