evidence_items.summary: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
evidence_items.title: DisasterVLG: Vision-Language Grounding and Evidence-Based Reasoning for Disaster Scene Understanding

evidence_items.summary: LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicated detectors lead. We release the framework, an interactive leaderboard, and four datasets as a vendor-neutral basis for selecting safeguards under deployment constraints.
evidence_items.title: BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, synthetic data
evidence_items.summary: Learning everyday skills, like cooking a dish, relies increasingly on instructional media such as online videos. This opens the door to the use of video (and multimodal) large language models (LLMs) as task guidance assistants. A crucial capability for the real-world success of a prospective task guidance assistant is it's ability to intervene proactively as soon as a mistake is apparent in order to guide the user. To evaluate this crucial capability, we introduce Ego-MC-Bench (Mistake Corrections), a benchmark for evaluating reactive, step-by-step task guidance in realistic cooking scenarios. Extensive experiments show that Ego-MC-Bench is highly challenging for state-of-the-art video LLMs. We argue that a key reason is the limited availability of training data for fine-tuning models on this task. Although there exists a wide range of cooking video datasets, existing datasets lack examples of mistakes along with appropriately timed interventions. To help address this data limitation, we also introduce Ego-CoMist, a counterfactual synthetic dataset created by transforming non -interactive cooking videos into supervised training examples showing proactive interventions. We show that fine-tuning on Ego-CoMist yields performance gains especially for smaller and more efficient video LLMs that are well suited for delivering assistance on edge devices.
evidence_items.title: Streaming Interventions: Can Video Large Language Models Correct Mistakes as They Occur?

evidence_items.summary: Modern agricultural data is sourced from diverse platforms and spans multiple spatial scales, ranging from ground-level close-up photography to Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) aerial observation and satellite remote sensing imagery. Accordingly, agricultural multimodal reasoning demands robust cross-scale spatial understanding. However, due to the lack of multi-view agricultural benchmark datasets, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit severe ground-level bias, which leads to scale confusion then semantic collapse in agricultural perception tasks, such as misinterpreting farmland imagery as walls or floors. To address this, we introduce AgroOmni, a large-scale multi-view training corpus with 268,119 Visual Question Answering pairs covering 56 specialized task categories across 14 task types, designed to capture diverse scales in modern precision agriculture.Built on this dataset, we propose AgroNVILA, which achieves a new state-of-the-art of 59.86% on the AgroMind benchmark (+12.57 over GPT-5.2), effectively mitigating the multi-view cross-scale gap for holistic agricultural understanding. Diagnostic evaluations on AgMMU further reveal an inherent heterogeneity between macro-priors and micro-diagnostics through constrained zero-shot performance. Meanwhile, even minimal fine-tuning leads to a dramatic performance gain of AgroNVILA on AgMMU, strongly demonstrating its generalization capability empowered by AgroOmni. Full training scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/Jrookie2005/AgroOmni, and the AgroOmni dataset is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/AgroOmni/AgroOmni.
evidence_items.title: AgroOmni: A Large-Scale Multi-view Agricultural Dataset for Cross-Scale Multimodal Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .
evidence_items.title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.
evidence_items.title: A comprehensive benchmark and dual-encoder baseline for terraced field extraction in complex mountainous regions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Text-to-SQL systems allow users to query databases in natural language, yet existing benchmarks cover English and a small number of well-resourced languages, and no resource has been reported for Kurdish. This paper presents SoraniSQL, a novel dataset and benchmark that is, to the best of current knowledge, the first for Text-to-SQL in Central Kurdish (Sorani). The dataset contains 7,518 question-SQL pairs from 609 query types, systematically constructed over a nine-table retail point-of-sale database with four database instances for test-suite execution accuracy (EXₜₛ); a five-member native-speaker panel rated a stratified sample of 200 questions at 4.9 out of 5 for fluency and 4.9 for adequacy. Dedicated splits separate new values, unseen phrasings, unseen combinations of query components, unseen SQL constructs and spelling variation. Experiments with retrieval, template, compositional, neural and pretrained models, all tuned on development data, show that a template classifier reaches 97.1% EXₜₛ on new values but 0.7% on unseen combinations, where a compositional model reaches 97.7%. A 1.5B-parameter code model fine-tuned with quantised low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) reaches 95.0% on unseen combinations on a laptop central processing unit (CPU), and the structure split and the orthographic-noise sets form the most demanding conditions of the benchmark. A Windows application, DanaText2SQL, demonstrates offline use of the benchmark's best fast model with Microsoft SQL Server.
evidence_items.title: SoraniSQL: A Novel Synthetic Text-to-SQL Dataset and Benchmark for Low-Resource Central Kurdish (Sorani)

organizations: International University of Business Agriculture and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is based on accumulated precipitation, but there is a difference between the scale of accumulation and the forecast lead time. When a forecast is issued at month t and verified at t+h-1, each post-issue month during the target accumulation period must either be forecast or be provided via a specified alternative. Although the method for constructing the SPI from observed and forecast precipitation is well established in operational practice, its impact on comparisons of lead times across different models has rarely been quantified. We assess three accumulation methods; a full-trajectory forecast, a climatology-gap operational baseline, and a perfect-intermediate-information (PII) diagnostic. This study uses a dataset comprising 10 stations with complete records from Bangladesh, six expanding rolling-origin folds, ten forecasting techniques, SPI values of 3, 6 and 12 months, and lead times of 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Sensitivity analyses were carried out on a 34-station dataset with variable records and an empirical SPI. For the Gamma SPI-12, the difference between the PII and full-trajectory approaches increased with lead time and reaches +0.760 F1, +0.732 PR-AUC, and +1.873 R2. No method performed best in all criteria and simple baselines of climatology and residual-trees were highly competitive. This shows that the accumulation protocol can qualitatively affect the conclusions about lead-time skill and model performance.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Horizon SPI Drought Forecast Skill under Alternative Accumulation Protocols: A Rolling-Origin Benchmark for Bangladesh

organizations: College of Life Science and Technology, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing 100029, China

evidence_items.summary: Polyol sweeteners in sugar-free beverages can cause osmotic diarrhea after acute bolus intake. Reference points, mostly no-observed-adverse-effect levels, depend on tested doses and lack uncertainty intervals. A systematic search yielded eight datasets covering six polyols; six datasets (five polyols) formed the primary analysis, with dose-escalation sorbitol data analyzed exploratorily. Bayesian model averaging at 10% extra risk yielded adult lower credible bounds on benchmark doses (BMDLs) of 0.400, 0.358, 0.162, 0.132, and 0.087 g/kg body weight for erythritol, maltitol, xylitol, isomalt, and lactitol, respectively; the pediatric erythritol BMDL was 0.552 g/kg body weight. Lowering the benchmark response to 5% reduced BMDLs by 44.4–53.7% without changing adult rankings. Using consumption and body-weight data, BMDLs were converted into concentrations. For a 20 kg child consuming 0.9 L once (uncertainty factor 1), reference concentrations were 1.9–12.2 g/L, inversely proportional to volume. Differences in matrices, endpoints, background incidences, and dose designs preclude definitive intrinsic potency ranking. Most estimates required low-dose extrapolation; except for erythritol, child scenarios used adult data without pediatric dose–response evidence. These concentrations are not safety or regulatory limits, formulation recommendations, individual no-effect thresholds, or concentrations validated to protect all children. Values derived from solid matrices require validation in beverages.
evidence_items.title: Reassessment of the Laxative Effects of Polyol Sweeteners Using Benchmark Dose Modeling, with an Analysis of Beverage Consumption Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Abstract De novo drug design must balance global drug properties with local structural determinants of target specificity. However, existing methods often reduce both objectives to local geometric optimization, relying on blind, reward-driven perturbations that can disrupt essential scaffolds and compromise overall drug-likeness. To resolve this destructive optimization trap, we propose CadreAI, a semantically decoupled agentic de novo drug design framework. CadreAI explicitly decomposes the entire drug design process into two independent subtasks: target-oriented semantic planning and plan-conditioned molecular generation. This strict separation mitigates potential task interference, allowing each module to focus exclusively on its dedicated objective without mutual disruption. Crucially, the strategic logic of how to formulate these target-oriented plans is driven by Simulation-Guided Insight Consolidation (SGIC). To eliminate trial-and-error guessing, this persistent memory mechanism translates transient numerical docking feedback into reusable textual heuristics, allowing the agent to continuously learn and logically deduce subsequent structural edits. Evaluated on the CrossDocked2020 and DrugGen benchmarks, molecules generated by CadreAI achieve superior docking performance with suitable drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. Additional Boltz-2 evaluations provide orthogonal computational validation of predicted structural plausibility and binding affinity. These results demonstrate that semantically decoupled reasoning offers a highly controllable and practical route for in silico therapeutic design.
evidence_items.title:
CadreAI: Agentic
AI for Semantically Decoupled Protein–Drug
Design and Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Securing the Internet of Things (IoT) requires detecting and responding to evolving threats across distributed devices with limited computing and communication resources. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret security alerts and help investigate incidents. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends these capabilities by combining reasoning, planning, memory, and tool use to coordinate security actions. Existing studies offer a fragmented account of how these capabilities fit IoT architectures, what risks arise when agents act autonomously, and how to evaluate their performance. This survey addresses these gaps by tracing the transition from LLM-assisted analysis to agentic defence across threat detection, triage, investigation, and response. We develop a unified taxonomy covering IoT infrastructure, LLM-driven and agentic security, trust and resilience, application domains, and evaluation methods. We compare hierarchical, orchestration-based, distributed multi-agent, and cognitive architectures by examining where security decisions are made, how agents coordinate, and where actions are executed across device, edge, fog, and cloud layers. We also examine threats introduced by agentic operation, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, and compromised trust between agents, together with corresponding defences. Our synthesis finds that limited attack testing and dataset coverage leave uncertainty about how well these systems generalize, while coordination failures and inference overhead constrain deployment. These findings motivate research on trustworthy orchestration, privacy-preserving collaboration, explainable security decisions, and efficient edge inference.
evidence_items.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Agentic AI for IoT Security: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Curated datasets of real-world software bugs support empirical research in software testing, debugging, and automated program repair. However, exploring heterogeneous bug collections, comparing fault characteristics across projects, and constructing research-specific subsets often require manual inspection and custom scripts. We present TSBugs Explorer, an interactive visual analytics platform built upon our previously-published dataset of 633 bugs from 16 open-source TypeScript repositories, classified into 11 fault categories. The platform integrates bug records, repository characteristics, dependency information, and taxonomy guidance through coordinated visualizations, interactive filtering, and detailed bug inspection. It supports alternative aggregation and normalization of fault distributions, pairwise repository comparisons, and analysis of differences in observed fault profiles. An integrated benchmark builder allows researchers to select bug subsets using multiple criteria, inspect their composition, and export records in CSV or JSON format. We demonstrate the platform through three research workflows: fault characterization, cross-repository comparison, and task-specific benchmark construction. Functional validation by two authors confirmed selection correctness, visualization consistency, export integrity, and reproducibility across the tested workflows. By making the existing corpus easier to explore, compare, and reuse, TSBugs Explorer facilitates systematic, research-specific selection and export of TypeScript bug records.
evidence_items.title: TSBugs Explorer: Exploring and Benchmarking TypeScript Bugs

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.
evidence_items.title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Autograders are a standard tool for evaluating student submissions in programming courses. However, proof-based and short-answer questions characteristic of Computer Science theory courses make grading a substantially more complex and labor-intensive task. In courses such as Discrete Mathematics, teaching assistants and instructors may dedicate several hours per week solely to grading, reducing the time available for higher-impact student interactions such as office hours. Large language models (LLMs) present a promising avenue for alleviating this burden, though their efficacy in this domain remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we evaluate a suite of LLMs for Discrete Mathematics grading. We introduce IADMD (Instructor-Annotated Discrete Mathematics Dataset), a benchmark of over 100 problems drawn from a second-year undergraduate course. To mitigate privacy concerns, synthetic student responses are generated by an LLM and subsequently edited and graded by a current Discrete Mathematics course instructor. A second expert grader separately annotated 12% of the examples to establish inter-rater reliability. Our findings indicate that LLMs can match or even exceed agreement observed between two human graders, suggesting their readiness for real-world integration into course grading workflows. We nonetheless advise instructors to assess model suitability for their specific course before adoption.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Language Models for Discrete Mathematics Grading

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM).


METHODS
Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings.


RESULTS
Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM.


CONCLUSIONS
BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.
evidence_items.title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge.

evidence_items.summary: To help students understand Human-In-The-Loop in AI and how human biases affect AI outcomes, we developed an AI4K12 software called WiseSpend AI. This is a browser-based educational game that places middle school students in the role of data labeler and AI trainer. Students classify household items as financial Needs or Wants to train a rule-based classifier, then evaluate that classifier's autonomous decisions across a simulated 30-day budget challenge. This game provides students with a first-person experience in training data quality, model generalization, and human-AI trust. We tested the game in a middle school setting and analyzed 15,567 logged interaction events from 89 students across 117 sessions combined with 143 pre-activity survey responses. Our findings show that students learned best by actively training the AI, and their outcomes were driven more by the quality and balance of that training than by prior AI knowledge or in-game spending. They also tended to over-trust the AI at first, but replay and hands-on iteration helped them improve at both judging the model and improving its behavior. Students showed clear signs of learning during gameplay, with many shifting from personal preference to thinking carefully about what examples the AI actually needed. One student described this as ''starving my robot'' when they realized they hadn't given it enough examples in the ''Need'' category. Features like the real- time Confidence Meter helped students catch and fix their AI's mistakes. These results suggest that simple, browser-based games can effectively build student understanding of data, fairness, and responsibility in AI systems.
evidence_items.title: WiseSpend AI: Engaging K-12 Students in Financial Literacy by Evaluating the Human Role in Training Artificial Intelligence
