evidence_items.summary:
PURPOSE
Total body irradiation (TBI) is an integral component of conditioning regimens for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Despite similar biological objectives, planning and delivery of TBI vary substantially across institutions. The aim of this study was to quantitatively assess inter-institutional and technique-dependent variability in contemporary TBI planning by comparing dose distributions generated under standardized conditions across multiple centers in Germany and Switzerland.


METHODS
Twenty-four radiotherapy centers received anonymized total-body computed tomography (CT) datasets of a standardized dummy patient in head-first supine and prone orientations, including predefined points of interest (POI) and organs at risk (OARs). Each center was asked to generate TBI plans for two prescription levels (8 Gy in 4 fractions and 12 Gy in 6 fractions) using its local planning standards, with the entire body defined as the planning target volume (PTV). Submissions included treatment-planning-system (TPS)-based 3D dose distributions and in-house table-based calculations. TPS plans were centrally imported into a TPS for extraction of target coverage and OAR dose metrics, while table-based submissions were evaluated using aggregated POI doses.


RESULTS
In total, 45 TBI treatment plans from 24 centers were analyzed, including 24 plans for 8 Gy and 21 plans for 12 Gy. Both TPS-based and table-based planning approaches were represented across a broad range of clinical techniques, including volumetic modulated arc therapy (VMAT), Tomotherapy, sweeping beam, static field, bilateral, and translation couch setups. Marked inter-institutional variability was observed, particularly for lung, lens, and kidney doses. At the 12 Gy prescription level, mean lung doses differed by more than 3 Gy between centers, corresponding to relative variations of up to approximately 30%. Conformal intensity-modulated techniques (VMAT and Tomotherapy) showed the highest consistency across institutions, whereas non-conformal approaches exhibited substantially larger dose variability. Increased lung sparing at 12 Gy was consistently associated with reduced target coverage compared to 8 Gy.


CONCLUSION
This study provides the first standardized multicenter planning-based comparison of contemporary TBI approaches in Germany and Switzerland. By quantifying inter-institutional variability in dose distributions under uniform conditions, the results outline the current heterogeneity of clinical practice and the range of achievable dosimetric outcomes. Rather than defining a reference standard, these findings establish a structured benchmark of existing planning strategies and highlight the need for harmonization, thereby providing a foundation for future consensus development and end-to-end validation efforts.
evidence_items.title: Multicenter evaluation of total body irradiation planning strategies: A DGMP working group study on large-field irradiation techniques.

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
Detecting heartbeats in photoplethysmography (PPG) underlies heart-rate, heart-rate-variability and arrhythmia analysis on wearable and clinical devices, and must be both efficient and accurate. Several accurate benchmark detectors, especially the multi-scale peak-and-trough family (MSPTD/MSPTDfast), rely on costly local-maxima scalograms; we seek a detector that improves the benchmark-wide speed-accuracy trade-off rather than merely accelerating one baseline. Approach: MorphSSF converts each PPG window to a slope-sum function (SSF), estimates the dominant pulse period from a band-limited autocorrelation, and selects candidates as fixed points of a period-matched running-maximum dilation on the SSF. This combines systolic-upstroke enhancement with adaptive period spacing using one-dimensional operations and no scalogram. We evaluate under identical conditions on seven datasets (544 recordings) with benchmark-wide rank tests, detector-specific exclusions and one-to-one matching. Separate fixed-point C and causal MATLAB variants are evaluated. Main results: MorphSSF has the best mean dataset F1 rank. Against MSPTDfast (v2), sensitivity tests favour MorphSSF on five datasets (including a zero median effect on CapnoBase); F1 is higher on MIMIC-test, MIMIC-train and PPG-DaLiA, while positive predictive value (PPV) is lower on WESAD. Both pooled and equal-dataset analyses favour MorphSSF in F1 against all eight baselines. MorphSSF is 3.05-218.18× faster than the eight baselines, including 3.23× faster than MSPTDfast (v2), based on median runtime ratios across recordings. All detectors receive the same prefiltered PPG input, with this shared filtering step excluded from runtime measurements. Significance: Period-adaptive detection on the slope-sum provides an efficient, scalogram-free approach to PPG beat detection. .
evidence_items.title: MorphSSF: a fast slope-sum adaptive-period dilation algorithm for photoplethysmography beat detection.

evidence_items.summary: Cadaveric dissection is a traditional method used to reveal deep-seated anatomical structures; however, it is inherently time-consuming and irreversible, preventing the correction of procedural errors. To address these limitations, this feasibility study proposes a novel computer-assisted, “digital dissection” framework designed to accelerate workflow, allow error mitigation, and enable repeatable analysis of a single specimen. Four independent observers performed “digital dissections” of the inferior medial genicular artery across two DICOM viewing platforms: RadiANT DICOM Viewer 2025.2 (64-bit) and Horos v4.0.0 RC5. Morphometric measurements were recorded at predefined reference points corresponding to arterial branching sites. Inter-observer variability was evaluated, and the resulting dataset was validated against multiplanar reconstruction (MPR) metrics—the standard radiological benchmark for vascular assessment. Statistical analysis revealed no significant difference between three-dimensional volume rendering (3D VR) and MPR in assessing vessel dimensions for structures with a diameter exceeding (dMPR=0.950 mm). For vessels > 0.95 mm, 3D-VR and MPR yielded no statistically significant difference (p = 0.086), a strong Pearson correlation (r = 0.971), and a Bland‑Altman mean bias of −0.03 mm (95% LoA: − 0.14 to +0.07 mm). Furthermore, morphological consistency was maintained regardless of vessel caliber. The integration of 3D VR and MPR modalities would offer a cost-effective, highly reproducible, non-invasive tool for both educational and research applications in vascular analysis. Moreover, these measurements exhibit strong stability across different software platforms and operators, showing an absence of systematic bias with only minor variations attributable to human error or minor misalignment.
evidence_items.title: Multi-planar reconstruction and 3D volume rendering as tools of anatomical dissection and morphometry on the example of cadaveric study of inferior medial genicular artery

evidence_items.summary: Detecting synthetically generated speech has become increasingly important for forensic speaker verification and digital media security. In particular, recent advances in speech synthesis and voice conversion technologies have enabled the generation of increasingly natural speech samples that are difficult to distinguish from genuine human speech, rendering fake speech detection approaches based solely on perceptual cues insufficient and increasing the need for more robust automated detection systems. This has highlighted the importance of developing methods capable of revealing subtle synthesis artifacts that may not be readily perceptible to the human ear in the time-frequency domain, while jointly modeling patterns across multiple scales. This study investigates a hybrid deep learning model for audio deepfake detection, using a Constant-Q Transform (CQT) scalogram frontend alongside residual convolutional blocks, spatial self-attention, and transformer encoders. This architecture is designed to capture both local spectral details and sequential patterns within audio recordings. Evaluations on the benchmark Fake-or-Real (FoR) dataset show that the proposed approach achieves an overall test accuracy of 94%, an AUROC score of 0.9919, and an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 3.86%, with a bootstrap analysis 95% confidence interval: 93.50–95.95%). These results demonstrate that combining time-frequency representations with attention mechanisms provides a stable decision framework for identifying speech spoofing attacks under standard evaluation protocols. The findings further demonstrate that, rather than relying on approaches based on a single feature extraction mechanism, hybrid architectures that jointly capture local spectral characteristics, attention-based regional information, and long-range temporal dependencies hold significant potential for audio deepfake detection. In this regard, the study provides a basis for the development of reliable and generalizable detection systems against increasingly sophisticated synthetic speech generation methods.
evidence_items.title: Audio deepfake detection using constant-Q transform scalograms and spatial-transformer attention networks

evidence_items.summary: Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI - a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.
evidence_items.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides.

evidence_items.summary: Analysis and experiment code accompanying the manuscript Can Scene-Level NWP Cloud Cover Replace Expert Pixel Labels? A Large-Scale Assessment with ERA5, GFS and CloudSEN12+ by Anna Anzalone and Antonio Pagliaro, submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI), 2026. The study asks whether freely available cloud-cover fields from numerical weather prediction (NWP) products can replace expensive expert pixel-level annotations when training cloud detectors for Sentinel-2. It has two parts: the collocation of ERA5 and GFS total cloud cover with 48,380 expert-annotated CloudSEN12+ patches spanning 2017-2022, and a set of controlled U-Net experiments on the official region-disjoint partition of the dataset, evaluated on 975 held-out expert-annotated patches, in which only the source of the training labels varies. The repository contains the download scripts for CloudSEN12+, ERA5 and GFS, the collocation and bootstrap statistics, the grouped bootstrap, the measurement of the ERA5 temporal offset, the collocation-scheme sensitivity test, and the U-Net training, evaluation and plotting scripts, together with a README mapping each script to the table or figure of the paper it produces. It also contains the collocation tables and the per-seed results of all 56 training runs. Version 2.0.0 corresponds to the revised manuscript.

evidence_items.summary: Tabular encoders are usually evaluated inside task-specific end-to-end pipelines, so models from different training paradigms are difficult to compare directly even when they operate on similar tabular signals. We introduce TRL-Bench, a multi-granular tabular representation learning (TRL) benchmark that standardizes cross-paradigm representation-level evaluation: each encoder exports row-, column-, or table embeddings through its supported wrapper, and shared lightweight heads probe them across three suites: TRL-CTbench (column/table), TRL-Rbench (row), and TRL-DLTE (compositional Data-Lake Table Enrichment spanning all three granularities). To support this standardized setting, we release curated benchmark assets and task reformulations, including 50 OpenML tables with 123 verified targets, 16 row-pair linkage rewrites, and a 47,772-table DLTE lake derived from 1,379 parent tables. Across 20 models and 16 tasks, TRL-Bench shows that once downstream conditions are standardized, encoder quality is capability-specific rather than captured by a single leaderboard. In TRL-CTbench, generic text encoders often lead on tasks with strong surface-text signal, while tabular specialists win where their pretraining objective aligns with the task. In TRL-Rbench, within-table prediction and cross-table linkage favor different training regimes, with atomic linkage performance correlating strongly with the row-matching stage of DLTE pipelines. In TRL-DLTE, the strongest pipelines combine capability-matched specialists rather than reuse a single encoder, and top end-to-end quality depends on non-additive compositional fit rather than per-stage marginal rank alone. TRL-Bench provides a common protocol for measuring reusable signal in exported tabular representations under shared downstream conditions. Code: https://github.com/LOGO-CUHKSZ/TRL-Bench; data is released on Hugging Face.
evidence_items.title: TRL-Bench: Standardizing Cross-Paradigm Representation-Level Evaluation of Tabular Encoders

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for optimization modeling and solver-code generation, yet practical operations research and optimization problems often require a harder capability: designing scalable algorithms that exploit problem structure and outperform direct formulation-and-solve baselines. Existing benchmarks are limited to small or simplified examples far below real-world scale and complexity. We introduce FrontierOR, the first literature-grounded benchmark targeting LLM-generated algorithm efficiency on realistic large-scale optimization problems. FrontierOR includes 180 diverse tasks, each derived from a paper published in a top-tier operations research venue, with standardized instances and a hidden, expert-verified evaluation suite. We evaluate recent LLMs' one-shot algorithm generation and improvements achieved through several self-evolving frameworks. The results show that current models still struggle to move from executable formulations to efficient optimization algorithms. Even the strongest LLM succeeds on only 39% of Full-set task instances, where success is defined as returning a feasible solution with an objective gap of at most 1% relative to Gurobi within its runtime. On the Hard subset, test-time evolution raises this proportion from 51% for the strongest one-shot model to 78%. FrontierOR provides a continuously maintained testbed for evaluating LLM-designed optimization algorithms under a shared protocol and controlled computational settings. Code and data are publicly released at https://github.com/Minw913/FrontierOR.
evidence_items.title: FrontierOR: Benchmarking LLMs' Capacity for Efficient Algorithm Design in Large-Scale Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but their ability to simulate individual privacy decisions is not well understood. In this paper, we evaluate whether a core set of user persona attributes can drive LLMs to simulate individual-level privacy behavior across various contexts. We introduce PrivacySIM, an evaluation suite that benchmarks LLM simulation of user privacy behavior against the ground-truth responses of 1,000 real users. These users are drawn from five published user studies on privacy behavior spanning LLM healthcare consultations, conversational agents, and chatbots. Drawing on these user studies and prior work in privacy behavior, we hypothesize three persona facets as plausible predictors of privacy decision-making: demographics, previous experiences, and stated privacy attitudes. We condition nine frontier LLMs on subsets of these three facets and measure how often each model's response to a data-sharing scenario matches the user's actual response. Our findings show that (1) zero-shot conditioning on these facets consistently improves simulation quality, but the performance of the best model (40.4% accuracy) suggests that richer and more nuanced persona facets are needed to reliably align with users' mental models for privacy decisions. (2) A user's stated privacy attitudes alone are often not the best predictor because they can diverge from the user's actual privacy behavior. (3) Users with high AI/chatbot experience are the most challenging to simulate. PrivacySIM is a first step toward understanding and improving the capabilities of LLMs to simulate user privacy decisions. We release PrivacySIM to enable further evaluation of LLM privacy simulation.
evidence_items.title: PrivacySIM: Evaluating LLM Simulation of User Privacy Behavior

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate chains of thought (CoTs) that are not always causally responsible for their final outputs. When such a mismatch occurs, the CoT no longer faithfully reflects the actual reasons (i.e., decision-critical factors) driving the model's behavior, leading to the reduced CoT monitorability problem. This limits the use of CoTs for reliable oversight. However, a comprehensive and fully open-source benchmark for thoroughly evaluating CoT monitorability remains lacking. To address this gap, we propose MonitorBench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating CoT monitorability in LLMs. MonitorBench provides: (1) a diverse set of 1,540 test instances with carefully designed decision-critical factors across 19 tasks spanning 7 categories to characterize when CoTs can be used to monitor the factors driving LLM behavior; and (2) two prompting stress-test settings to quantify the extent to which CoT monitorability can be degraded. Extensive experiments show that CoT monitorability is a conditional property affected by the evaluated LLM, monitor LLM, and task characteristics. Across these factors, monitorability is higher when decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning process, rather than merely influencing the final answer. Under stress-test prompting, most evaluated LLMs can intentionally reduce monitorability, mainly on tasks where decision-critical factors are not structurally required by the reasoning process. Overall, MonitorBench provides a basis for further research on AI control, reasoning faithfulness, stress-test monitorability, and monitoring scaffords. The code is available at https://github.com/ASTRAL-Group/MonitorBench.
evidence_items.title: MonitorBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.
evidence_items.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Autoscalers for large language model (LLM) inference clusters that add capacity when a predicted overload probability crosses a threshold depend on the probability scale, not only on the ranking. This simulation study evaluates five such predictors under sparse telemetry and runtime anomalies on two latent-state generators and a request-level serving simulator with queueing, service-level objectives (SLOs), startup delay, and modeled power. With 3-period instead of 50-period histories, models trained on long histories became overconfident (expected calibration error up to 0.099) or conservative, whereas a Markov filter stayed calibrated and retraining on short histories removed most of the error. Temperature scaling fitted on long histories did not transfer; refitted for short histories, it cut this error by up to 68.7%, removed all 290 wrong high-confidence predictions of one model by lowering their confidence, and cut the overconfident models' idealized unmitigated overload by 59.8–82.8% at the cost of more idle capacity. With a 20-s startup delay in the request-level simulator, learned predictors used 24.0–25.3% less modeled energy than always-on scale-out, with a 1.0–1.2 percentage-point increase in the SLO-violation rate, and 95.3% of scale-out-induced violations occurred on slow new replicas. Calibration should therefore be validated per telemetry regime and checked against request-level outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Predictive Reliability and Calibration of Workload Autoscaling Models for Large Language Model Inference Clusters Under Sparse Telemetry and Runtime Anomalies

evidence_items.summary: Widely accessible generative artificial intelligence has unsettled long held assumptions about how learning can be measured and trusted. Tools capable of producing fluent essays, functional code, and plausible solutions on demand have exposed the fragility of evaluation models that reward the unsupervised production of polished artifacts. This paper argues that the appropriate institutional response is not an escalating contest between detection software and evasion techniques, but a deliberate redesign of evaluation around authentic human competency. Drawing on established scholarship in authentic assessment, constructive alignment, and formative feedback, the paper develops a five-principle framework for evaluation that remains meaningful when capable AI is freely available. The framework shifts emphasis from the finished product toward the reasoning process, foregrounds contextual judgment that machines cannot convincingly simulate, distributes evidence of competency across a program rather than isolated high stakes events, treats AI as a declared and scrutinized instrument rather than prohibited contraband, and grounds security in thoughtful design rather than pervasive surveillance. Common assessment formats are appraised for their resilience, and implementation challenges relating to staff workload, equity of access, and institutional policy are examined. The paper concludes that the disruption introduced by generative AI, although genuinely destabilizing, presents an overdue opportunity to align evaluation with the competencies that human learners must actually develop, and to recover the formative purpose of assessment that narrow integrity policing has long obscured.
evidence_items.title: Assessment Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Redesigning Learning Evaluation for Authentic Human Competency

evidence_items.summary: Emergency radiology operates at the intersection of high imaging volumes, time-critical diagnoses, and persistent workforce shortages, making it one of the most promising yet demanding environments for artificial intelligence (AI) deployment. This narrative review critically appraises the evidence on AI in emergency radiology, emphasizing diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and the strength of the underlying evidence. We searched PubMed for peer-reviewed literature published between January 2015 and August 2026 using a structured, reproducible strategy, and we classified key studies by design and outcome level. Deep learning algorithms approach expert-level performance in retrospective and reader-study settings for several high-stakes conditions, including intracranial hemorrhage (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve up to 0.991), acute pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and skeletal fractures, for which a multicenter multireader diagnostic accuracy study found that AI assistance increased reader sensitivity by 10.4 percentage points and specificity from 90.6% to 95.6%. However, real-world evaluations report substantially lower sensitivity than development studies, and workflow evidence is mixed: in one prospective implementation, head CT studies flagged by AI for intracranial hemorrhage were interpreted sooner than routine studies (median 19 vs. 512 min), whereas a pulmonary embolism notification system produced no measurable turnaround benefit. Deep learning reconstruction can reduce radiation dose, and large language models show early promise for report error detection and communication. Prospective, multisite, patient-outcome evidence remains scarce. AI should be viewed as an augmenting technology whose value in emergency radiology depends on local validation, deliberate workflow integration, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency radiology: opportunities, evidence, and limitations

evidence_items.summary: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. A matched control that holds the retention mechanism fixed and swaps only the learning rule shows that backpropagation with the same generative replay reaches a comparable or slightly higher accuracy than LEL (90.3% vs.
evidence_items.title: Backpropagation-Free Continual Learning: A Unified Energy-Based Framework, Reproducible Benchmark, and Open Challenges

evidence_items.summary: When using the in situ nylon bag technique to evaluate rumen degradation characteristics, if the microbial contamination in the nylon bag residue is not corrected, the degradation rate of roughage nitrogen in rumen will be underestimated. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to determine the bacterial contamination of roughages during in situ rumen culture, and to establish an equation for predicting microbial contamination of rumen culture residue. Using the nylon bag technique, a total of 30 roughages was incubated in the rumen of four Zhaowuda meat sheep. (15NH4)2SO4 was continuously infused into the rumen, and then pellets of labeled rumen solids-associated bacteria (SAB) and rumen liquid-associated bacteria (LAB) were isolated by differential centrifugation of samples of ruminal contents. The rumen degradation rate of 24 kinds of roughage nitrogen was significantly increased after microbial correction (p < 0.05), six kinds of roughage nitrogen species were increased in numerical value although there was no significant difference (p > 0.05), and there was no difference between the two labeling methods of SAB and LAB. Except for imported alfalfa hay (AH), the course of bacterial contamination of 29 roughages was described by an exponential function of the general type Ncont. = Nmax [1 − exp(−C·t)], where Nmax varied with the feed’s nutritional composition. Separate prediction models were established for straw roughages, hay roughages, and all 29 roughages combined, incorporating crude protein (CP), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF), dry matter (DM), and organic matter (OM) to estimate Nmax. The results confirm that microbial contamination systematically biases nylon bag measurements, causing a consistent underestimation of true ruminal nitrogen degradability, especially for high-fiber, low-protein feeds.
evidence_items.title: Development of Equations to Estimate Microbial Nitrogen Contamination of In Situ Roughage Residues

evidence_items.summary: This work develops and benchmarks a numerical framework for computing decaying traveling-wave solutions of the Degasperis–Procesi equation. The approach provides a unified treatment of smooth solitary waves and peaked wave solutions across the relevant parameter regimes. Cusped and anticusped profiles are excluded, as their stronger singular behavior is not compatible with the regularity assumptions underlying the numerical formulation. The method addresses the challenges associated with the asymptotic behavior of the solutions and the non-smoothness of peaked profiles. Its performance is systematically assessed through convergence studies and comparisons with exact solutions. For smooth traveling waves, the numerical results exhibit the expected second-order convergence, while the computations for peaked waves demonstrate the method’s ability to resolve the non-smooth profile. The results also illustrate the dependence of wave profiles and amplitudes on wave speed and other model parameters, providing a benchmark for numerical computation of these solutions.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Computation of Smooth and Peaked Decaying Traveling-Wave Solutions of the Degasperis–Procesi Equation: A Benchmark Study

In the present study, the prediction model for compressive strength of plain weave fabric reinforced composites (PWFCs) is developed using an analytical solution for a three-layer laminate [0°/90°/0°] under uniaxial compression (σ

 x

Results are compared with tensile strength predictions from previous studies, and both Tsai-Hill and Tsai-Wu failure criteria are applied and benchmarked against literature values. The results revealed that for the [0°/90°/0°] layup, all compressive loading cases are governed by transverse matrix crushing in the 90° ply. The uniaxial compressive strength (136–144 MPa) is only 22–23% of the tensile strength (617 MPa). This large tension–compression asymmetry arises from the low transverse compressive strength (140 MPa) combined with stress concentration in the 90° layer. Further, under biaxial compression, failure occurs at just 28–33 MPa — a 77–80% reduction from uniaxial compressive strength and a 95% reduction from the tensile benchmark. Tsai-Wu predicts 5–14% lower failure loads than Tsai-Hill under compressive loading. The [0°/90°/0°] stacking is poorly optimized for compressive or biaxial loading; incorporating ±45° plies is recommended to improve biaxial compressive performance.
evidence_items.title: Compressive Strength Behaviour of Plain Weave Fabric Composites under Uniaxial and Biaxial Loading

evidence_items.summary: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a marine energy technology that utilizes the temperature difference between surface seawater and deep seawater to generate electricity. One of the main components in this system is the Cold Water Pipe (CWP), which functions to transport cold seawater from deep ocean layers to the power generation system. The long pipe structure with a large diameter-to-thickness ratio makes it susceptible to bending deformation. This study aims to analyze the effect of geometric imperfections on the bending capacity of CWP pipes using the Finite Element Method (FEM). The numerical model was validated through a benchmarking process against a bending formulation, with a deviation of 2.64%. A parametric study was conducted on circumferential imperfections in the form of sinusoidal waves with variations in amplitude and number of waves. The results show that increasing imperfection amplitude reduces the bending capacity, while increasing the number of waves tends to increase the ultimate moment value. This behavior is likely related to the denser wave distribution along the longitudinal direction of the pipe, which may create a local stiffness effect similar to a stiffener element, thereby improving the structural resistance against bending deformation. Variations in imperfection configuration result in changes in the UM value of up to 24.1%, indicating that imperfection characteristics have a significant influence on the bending response of the CWP structure.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Study on the Bending Behavior of OTEC Cold Water Pipes Considering Geometric Imperfections

evidence_items.summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to treat, highlighting the need for strategies that selectively deliver cytotoxic agents to tumor cells. Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2) has been proposed as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC, but non-antibody-based delivery formats remain underexplored. Using protein-SELEX, we identified T17, a high-affinity aptamer that specifically binds to TROP2, and conjugated it to monomethyl auristatin E through an MC-Val-Cit-PAB linker to generate the aptamer-drug conjugate T17-M. Preclinical evaluation in cellular and animal models showed that T17-M retained TROP2-dependent binding, underwent clathrin-mediated internalization and lysosomal processing, and suppressed tumor growth in cell-line-derived and patient-derived xenografts. T17-M also reduced liver metastasis and induced calreticulin exposure, ATP release, and HMGB1 secretion, consistent with immunogenic cell death. In immunocompetent models, T17-M promoted dendritic-cell activation and CD8+ T cell infiltration, while its combination with PD-1 blockade further enhanced tumor control and prolonged survival. These findings provide preclinical proof-of-concept for T17-M as an alternative TROP2-targeted drug-delivery strategy for PDAC.
evidence_items.title: A TROP2-targeting aptamer enables selective drug delivery and potent antitumor activity in pancreatic cancer.

evidence_items.summary: Here we use a large language model for the exploration of chemical space of transition metal complexes (TMCs), fine-tuning the open-source Llama-3.2-1B model with a variation of the SMILES string representation tailored for coordination chemistry. We identify several key molecular properties that are critical to produce valid TMCs which we use for prompt engineering, creating TMC-Llama models that generate unique, novel, and structurally validated TMCs at high success rates, and exceeding the performance of both standard benchmarks as well as state-of-the-art generative methods in the literature. We use the pydentate workflow, Density Functional Theory calculations, and other benchmark metrics to show that the TMC-Llama model generates new TMC chemistries that are physically realistic, synthetically plausible, and geometrically consistent with large datasets of known experimental TMCs. Our study lays the groundwork for future TMC-Llama generative model applications to discover new TMCs for functional materials for catalysis, photochemistry, medicine, and sustainability technologies.
evidence_items.title: Exploring transition metal complexes with large language models.

evidence_items.summary: Modern computer-assisted synthesis planning (CASP) systems show promise at generating chemically valid reaction steps but struggle to incorporate strategic considerations such as convergent assembly, protecting-group minimization, and optimal ring-forming sequences. We introduce a methodology that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to distill synthetic knowledge into code. Our system analyzes synthesis routes and translates strategic principles into executable Python functions representing diverse strategic and tactical rules, such as strategic functional group interconversions, protecting strategies and ring construction features. We validate the use of LLM-as-a-judge in this domain, demonstrating their efficacy in evaluating synthesis-specific code generation. By formalizing this knowledge as verifiable code rather than simple heuristics, we create testable, interpretable representations of synthetic strategy. We release the complete codebase and the USPTO-ST data set─synthesis routes annotated with strategic tags. This framework unlocks a novel capability for CASP: natural language-based route retrieval, achieving 74.5% Top-3 accuracy on our benchmark. We further validate our library through temporal analysis of historical trends and chemically intuitive route clustering that offers more granular partitioning than common previous methods. This work bridges the tactical-strategic divide in CASP, enabling specification, search, and evaluation of routes by strategic criteria rather than structure alone.
evidence_items.title: SynthStrategy: Extracting and Formalizing Latent Strategic Insights from LLMs in Organic Chemistry.

evidence_items.summary: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.
evidence_items.title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents

evidence_items.summary:
The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has transformed information retrieval, yet limited understanding of its differences from traditional search engines hinders clarity regarding changes in user search behavior and variations in search effectiveness, thereby impeding guidance for future search interface design.
 
 
 
 We conducted a laboratory experiment comparing two versions of the Bing search engine: the traditional Bing search and the generative-AI integrated Bing (Bing Chat). We interpreted variations in user search behavior through querying, browsing, and clicking data, and established a multidimensional metric framework encompassing user, cost-benefit, and system dimensions to assess search effectiveness. 40 participants with good search skills completed the experiment, resulting in a final dataset comprising 160 observation records.
 
 
 
 The Mann-Whitney U test revealed that users of generative AI search engines exhibited the following characteristics compared to those using traditional search engines: longer queries, more keyboard activity, more frequent query restructuring (including more narrowing queries, more following the system queries, and more changing the syntactic structure queries, with less broadening queries), more browsing during the first search session, and less scrolling and clicking. The results of the Linear Mixed Models show that, compared to traditional search engines, users achieve superior performance with generative AI search on users’ subjective perceptions and search efficiency metrics. Furthermore, we employed machine learning to validate which search behaviors can predict a user’s search effectiveness. The results indicate that the Gradient Boosting Machines are the optimal prediction models. The five most significant indicators for predicting search performance are Avelength. QueryConsTime, TimetofirSearch, ResViewTime and NumbofScroll.
 
 
 
 By revealing differences in user behavior and search efficiency across various search engines, this study deepens our understanding of generative AI search engines at a finer granularity and contributes to building adaptive search platforms capable of optimizing search recommendations.
 
 
 
 By revealing differences in user behavior and efficiency between traditional and generative versions of the Bing search engine, this study deepens our understanding of generative AI search engines at a finer granularity and contributes to building adaptive search platforms capable of optimizing search recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Effectiveness evaluation of generative intelligent search: a comparative study with traditional search engine

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education for assessment, tutoring, learning analytics, resource production and academic administration. An emerging area is the use of generative systems for music business education. Artists and Repertoire (A&R) professionals play a central role in finding new musical talent, shaping artistic direction, and connecting artists with songwriters and music producers. Preparing music business students for this role typically requires them to engage with real world artists, with whom they can develop their interviewing and other A&R skills. Using role play during the early stages of teaching can support students with developing their skills before they work with real artists. In this study, Ama, a fictional R&B and neo-soul musician realised through an embodied conversational agent, underwent preliminary design and formative evaluation. The agent was developed as an interactive rehearsal partner for students learning about the artists and repertoire process. Development involved using a combination of generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Copilot, Kling AI, Suno, Nano Banana, and Adobe Firefly, to develop the artist's lyrics and supporting media, thereby visualising the artist. Her profile was extended into a knowledge base, configuring the agent and refining its responses. The evaluation identified issues relating to response length, answer format, conversational naturalness, generative improvisation and latency. The study presents a prototype developed through iterative design, providing preliminary results and a foundation for further research with students using embodied conversational agents in the classroom.
evidence_items.title: Embodied Conversational Agents as Rehearsal Partners for Developing Music Business Students' A&R Skills

evidence_items.summary: AI-driven adaptive learning environments are transforming per- sonalized education, yet most tutoring systems lack personality- aware feedback tailored to individual learning preferences. This paper presents a usability study evaluating Casey, an AI-powered conversational agent that dynamically assesses students' Big Five personality traits and adapts instructional support accordingly. Us- ing a mixed-methods approach (including interaction metrics and qualitative feedback), user engagement, perceived usability, and the impact of personality-based adaptation in coding education are analyzed. Findings reveal that personalized feedback may enhance engagement but also introduces usability challenges, particularly in balancing real-time guidance, cognitive load, and user auton- omy. The results provide actionable insights for improving adaptive tutoring systems by optimizing feedback clarity, navigation, and learner control. This work contributes to the field of AI-driven edu- cation by informing the design of intelligent tutoring systems that can enhance both engagement and usability at scale.
evidence_items.title: Exploring the Usability of Personality-Aware Conversational Agents in Intelligent Tutoring System

evidence_items.summary:
Bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, has become a mainstay in the management of malignant gliomas. Multiple bevacizumab biosimilars have been approved since initial FDA approval of the reference agent and have seen widespread use, in part due to reduced costs. However, real-world data evaluating comparability between reference and biosimilar agents, especially for the management of glioblastoma, remain limited.
 
 
 
 We performed a retrospective analysis of patients treated with reference bevacizumab (Avastin ®) versus those receiving bevacizumab-bvzr (Zirabev ®), a widely used biosimilar agent for the management of IDH wild-type glioblastoma at our institution between 2019 and 2022. Outcomes of interest included rates of dose-limiting adverse effects associated with anti-angiogenic therapy, as well as survival as measured by overall survival (OS).
 
 
 
 A total of 129 patients were included in our final analysis; 71 received reference drug (bevacizumab) while 58 received the biosimilar agent (bevacizumab-bvzr). Rates of dose-limiting adverse effects were similar between both groups (OR 1.2013, p = 0.7418). On analysis of the entire cohort, concomitant treatment with anticoagulation (OR 3.3045, p = 0.0238) was associated with a higher risk of dose-limiting adverse effects On survival analysis, we found that OS was similar between the bevacizumab (median OS 714 daysdays) and biosimilar (median OS 631 days) groups by both univariate (p = 0.5639). and multivariate (HR 1.0869, p = 0.6916) analyses.
 
 
 
 Bevacizumab-bvzr demonstrated similar clinical efficacy and safety profile compared to reference bevacizumab in our institutional cohort of IDH-WT glioblastoma patients.
evidence_items.title: Real-world outcomes of biosimilar bevacizumab-bvzr versus reference agent in the management of patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than assessing the distinct clinical responsibilities along longitudinal care pathways. We introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from real-world records of 405 patients at two cancer centers, it comprises 941 evaluation units across six sequential care stages, from work-up through follow-up, and 17,688 patient-specific criteria across five dimensions. Each assessment is restricted to clinical evidence available at the corresponding decision point. Across 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, we find strong diagnostic scores did not ensure reliable downstream care. Decision Quality ranged from 56.8 to 94.7 in diagnosis on a 0-100 scale, but dropped to 8.9-56.0 in staging and spanned 32.4-94.2 in treatment. Crucially, failure modes differed across phases: explicit decision errors predominated in anatomical staging (48.2%), whereas decision omissions were more frequent during initial work-up (33.4%) and post-treatment follow-up (30.4%). Varying query granularity revealed a trade-off between decision quality and other clinical requirements. Broad open-ended requests reduced decision quality across all 30 models, whereas more detailed, checklist-like prompts improved decision quality but were accompanied by lower evidence faithfulness and safety adherence. These findings highlight the need to assess clinical reliability against the distinct clinical requirements of each phase along the longitudinal care pathway. Finally, NPC-RubricBench informs the design of stage-aware clinical guardrails and offers a reusable blueprint for evaluating LLMs across other cancers and chronic diseases.
evidence_items.title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

evidence_items.summary: As polarization grows on social media, understanding how political memes shape online narratives has become increasingly important. Previous research has relied on either qualitative frameworks that are hard to scale or computational methods that lack theoretical grounding. Both approaches treat narrative categories in isolation and focus exclusively on moral portrayals of identity. To address these limitations, we introduce a framework grounded in social science theories, encompassing three categories: social identities (such as gender, politics, and ethnicity), viewpoints (ingroup and outgroup perspectives), and narrative roles (moral character, intelligence, appearance, and power). Building on this framework, we present IRON-Meme, a human-annotated benchmark comprising 1,110 political memes across substantially more templates than existing benchmarks. Our analysis of IRON-Meme shows that most memes assign derogatory roles and that identities, roles, and templates are systematically interconnected. Evaluation of nine vision-language models indicates that frontier-scale and reasoning models achieve the highest performance, while accuracy on social identities and narrative roles decreases for less frequent labels. Incorporating template background knowledge does not enhance narrative role classification, suggesting that meme interpretation relies on how memes are adapted for specific communicative purposes. We make IRON-Meme and our code publicly available.
evidence_items.title: IRON-Meme: A Benchmark for Structured Understanding of Identities and Roles in Online Meme Narratives

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.
evidence_items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching

evidence_items.summary: Reliable visual question answering requires correct answers when evidence is sufficient and abstention when it is not. We introduce a benchmark of 3,000 question groups: 1,000 each from PlotQA charts, CLEVR rendered scenes, and GQA photographs. Each group keeps the question fixed across original, answer-preserving, and evidence-removing images; charts and CLEVR also include answer-changing edits. Models receive each image independently. A group succeeds only if every supported answer and every required abstention is correct. For charts and CLEVR, executable witnesses establish ambiguity under the declared task semantics: two admissible complete charts or scenes give different answers but yield the same masked observation. GQA scoring compares source labels with a permissive rule that also credits masked-image answers compatible with the full-image reference. Across 72,000 responses from six model configurations, the best complete-question success is 57.0% on charts, 43.5% on CLEVR, and 33.7% on GQA under source labels. On charts, the strongest configuration makes correct answer-or-abstain decisions on 96.2% of individual images and on all five images of 83.5% of questions. Requiring correct answers lowers success to 57.0%: in 26.5% of all chart questions, every decision is correct but at least one answer is wrong. Adding answer correctness also reverses a chart ranking based on decision accuracy. Evaluating all response obligations together reveals failures that per-image decision accuracy conceals.
evidence_items.title: When Does an Image Determine the Answer? Benchmarking Visual Answerability across Charts and Scenes

evidence_items.summary: Rendering accurate text remains difficult for image generation and editing models, especially when the target contains long, complex, and densely arranged text or rare characters. Existing approaches either improve native text rendering through stronger backbones and data-centric training without explicit glyph priors, or incorporate glyph priors through specialized designs that remain insufficiently accurate and robust under challenging scenarios. We introduce GlyphAnchor, a novel text-rendering enhancement method for both text-to-image and image-editing diffusion transformer models. GlyphAnchor enhances the backbone with lightweight glyph patch conditions whose positions are anchored to the target image through the model's native positional encoding. We train this capability with staged supervised finetuning and further refine it with text-aware post-training to improve robustness. We also introduce InfoTextBench, a benchmark for evaluating text-rich visual text rendering in both generation and editing settings. Experiments across multiple backbones and benchmarks, including long, complex, and densely arranged text and rare character scenarios, show that GlyphAnchor consistently improves text fidelity while preserving overall image quality.
evidence_items.title: GlyphAnchor: Enhancing Visual Text Rendering via Position-Anchored Glyph Priors

evidence_items.summary: Longitudinal personal albums are weak-schema multimodal databases: noisy perceptual records whose key facts require joins across faces, text, timestamps, locations, and repeated events. Existing visual, video, document, and lifelog benchmarks test sub-problems, but not album-scale profile reconstruction with social identity binding and evidence citation. Benchmarking this task is difficult because the ground truth needed for evaluation--owner profiles, social graphs, face-name maps, and evidence provenance--is private state that real albums cannot safely release. We introduce PAL-Bench, a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded reconstruction under a public-record contract. Its Evidence Compiler builds latent private worlds, programs target-level evidence paths, renders album pixels, re-measures them through perception pipelines, and exports audited public/private views. Agents receive only perception-derived public records; targets, identifier maps, and evidence paths remain hidden. PAL-Bench contains 50 synthetic users, 36,659 public photo records, and 2,799 targets over owner facts, identities, and relations. A privacy-preserving audit with 10 participants confirms that PAL-Bench evidence structures match real private albums, though equivalent releases remain privacy-prohibitive. Across seven systems and two compute-matched diagnostics, a seven-metric protocol reveals a gap between plausible profile summarization and faithful social reconstruction: systems recover some owner facts but struggle with recurring identities and evidence citation. PAL-TRACE, a reference framework that freezes identity bindings before owner-fact mining, performs best but leaves hard identity resolution far from solved. PAL-Bench provides a testbed for perceptual entity resolution, multimodal data integration, temporal evidence aggregation, and provenance-aware structured prediction.
evidence_items.title: PAL-Bench: Evidence-Grounded Profile Reconstruction from Longitudinal Personal Albums

evidence_items.summary: Although the study of human trajectory anomalies is vital for spatial data mining, empirical research remains constrained by the lack of ground-truth datasets. Despite the availability of several real-world and simulated human trajectory datasets, most only include normal mobility patterns and lack annotated anomalies. This limitation primarily arises because anomalous events are rare in the real world and difficult to collect. Furthermore, collecting large-scale mobility data is hindered by strict privacy regulations and acquisition costs. To overcome these limitations and establish an explainable human trajectory anomalies dataset with annotated ground truth, we introduce an end-to-end generative framework designed to synthesize context-aware trajectory anomalies at scale. Unlike existing models, our framework applies real-world physical constraints on baseline simulated trajectories. We employ Large Language Model (LLM) agents to systematically inject semantically meaningful behavioral anomalies such as irregular out-of-distribution check-ins and skipped routine visits. To ensure the spatial validity, the system leverages a map-constrained routing module to recalculate the physical transitions between these LLM agent-modified staypoints. Moreover, to narrow the simulation-to-reality gap, we augment the resulting trajectories with a context-aware spatial noise model, parameterized by environmental and location-specific variables, to emulate heterogeneous GPS sensor degradation. Through this pipeline, our framework produces a CTI & EBI formatted mobility dataset with annotated anomalies, providing a benchmark for downstream spatial data mining tasks.
evidence_items.title: Synthesizing Human Trajectory Anomalies: An LLM-Driven Framework with Map-Constrained Routing and Sensor Noise Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Scientific research proceeds through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and revision. AI agents can automate parts of this process, but existing approaches typically follow a single research trajectory or coordinate through a central planner with fixed objectives. As a result, they struggle to sustain parallel exploration, adapt as experimental evidence changes, or preserve knowledge of failed directions over long-running experiments. We introduce AutoScientists, a decentralized team of AI agents for long-running computational scientific experimentation. Agents interpret a shared experimental state, self-organize into teams around promising hypotheses, critique proposals before using experimental compute, and share successes and failures to reduce redundant exploration. Under matched experimental budgets, AutoScientists improves over prior AI agents across biomedical machine learning, language-model training optimization, and protein fitness prediction. On BioML-Bench, spanning biomedical imaging, protein engineering, single-cell omics, and drug discovery, AutoScientists achieves a mean leaderboard percentile of 74.4% across 24 tasks, improving over the strongest AI agent by +8.33%. On GPT training optimization, AutoScientists reaches a target validation bits-per-byte 1.9x faster than Autoresearch and continues discovering improvements from a starting champion where the single-agent approach finds none (7 vs. 0 accepted improvements). On ProteinGym fitness prediction, AutoScientists discovers a method for ACE2-Spike binding that improves over the current state-of-the-art model by +12.5% in Spearman correlation. Applied without modification across all 217 ProteinGym assays, the same method improves over the prior state of the art by +6.5% (Spearman correlation).
evidence_items.title: AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation

evidence_items.summary: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.
evidence_items.title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images

evidence_items.summary: Data-driven approaches like deep learning are rapidly advancing planetary science, particularly in Mars exploration. Despite recent progress, most existing benchmarks remain confined to closed-set supervised visual tasks and do not support text-guided retrieval for geospatial discovery. We introduce MarsRetrieval, a retrieval benchmark for evaluating vision-language models for Martian geospatial discovery. MarsRetrieval includes three tasks: (1) paired image-text retrieval, (2) landform retrieval, and (3) global geo-localization, covering multiple spatial scales and diverse geomorphic origins. We propose a unified retrieval-centric protocol to benchmark multimodal embedding architectures, including contrastive dual-tower encoders and generative vision-language models. Our evaluation shows MarsRetrieval is challenging: even strong foundation models often fail to capture domain-specific geomorphic distinctions. We further show that domain-specific fine-tuning is critical for generalizable geospatial discovery in planetary settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-stat-Sustech/MarsRetrieval
evidence_items.title: MarsRetrieval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Planetary-Scale Geospatial Retrieval on Mars

evidence_items.summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting has emerged as a new paradigm for dynamic scene representation, enabling real-time rendering of scenes with complex motions. However, it faces a major challenge of storage overhead, as millions of Gaussians are required for high-fidelity reconstruction. Compressing explicit 4D Gaussians is challenging because they exhibit heterogeneous redundancy across static and dynamic regions, and their temporal attributes make direct quantization unstable. In this work, we present OMG4 (Optimized Minimal 4D Gaussian Splatting), a framework that constructs a compact set of salient Gaussians capable of faithfully representing 4D Gaussian models. Our method progressively reduces Gaussians in three stages: (1) Gaussian Sampling to identify primitives critical to reconstruction fidelity, (2) Gaussian Pruning to remove redundancies, and (3) Gaussian Merging to fuse primitives with similar characteristics. In addition, we integrate implicit appearance compression and extend Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) to 4D representations with a staged quantization scheme, further reducing storage while preserving quality. Extensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that OMG4 achieves a favorable rate-distortion trade-off over recent state-of-the-art methods, reducing model sizes by over 60% while maintaining reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of OMG4 as a practical framework for compact and high-fidelity 4D scene representation. Our source code is available at https://minshirley.github.io/OMG4/.
evidence_items.title: Optimized Minimal 4D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Dynamic Scene Representation

evidence_items.summary: Existing long-context benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) focus on evaluating comprehension of long inputs, while overlooking the evaluation of long reasoning abilities. To address this gap, we introduce LongReasonArena, a benchmark specifically designed to assess the long reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Our tasks require models to solve problems by executing multi-step algorithms that reflect key aspects of long reasoning, such as retrieval and backtracking. By controlling the inputs, the required reasoning length can be arbitrarily scaled, reaching up to 1 million tokens of reasoning for the most challenging tasks. Extensive evaluation results demonstrate that LongReasonArena presents a significant challenge for both open-source and proprietary LLMs. For instance, even GPT-5 achieves only 27.8% accuracy on Level 3. Further analysis also reveals that the accuracy exhibits a linear decline with respect to the logarithm of the expected number of reasoning steps. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/LongReasonArena/LongReasonArena.
evidence_items.title: LongReasonArena: A Long Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
evidence_items.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications

evidence_items.summary: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
evidence_items.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain

evidence_items.summary: Reproducibility archive for the manuscript "CMIP6 biogeochemical models under-represent the deep chlorophyll maximum and diverge in how they express it: a regime-based BGC-Argo evaluation in the North Pacific" (submitted to Biogeosciences; manuscript egusphere-2026-4562). Using quality-controlled BGC-Argo chlorophyll profiles over the North Pacific, the study evaluates the vertical chlorophyll structure of nine CMIP6 biogeochemical models and tests whether agreement in surface chlorophyll implies agreement in the vertical allocation of chlorophyll. Contents: - data/: analysis-ready CSV tables from a deterministic builder. - code/: the scripts that produce the figures, Table S1 and the numbers of Sect. 4.5 of the article (the preprocessing code that derives the analysis-ready tables from the source data is not included). - figures/: the figures of the article, its appendix, and its supplement. Raw BGC-Argo, CMIP6, satellite, and map source data are not redistributed in this archive. They are available from their original sources: the Argo Global Data Assembly Centre; ESGF (CMIP6 variable chl, table Omon, experiment historical, for the nine models listed in the archived README); the SEANOE physiological look-up table (https://doi.org/10.17882/105732); and standard map/coastline sources. The factor-two chlorophyll reference is Roesler et al. (2017), https://doi.org/10.1002/lom3.10185. Archive DOI (concept, resolves to the latest version): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20997630. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The associated article DOI will be added upon publication. v1.0.1: Figure 2 panels re-rendered with corrected inter-row panel spacing and left-column placement (figure layout only; data, values, colour scales, and all other figures unchanged). v1.1.0: The figures have been fully redesigned for a regime-stratified analysis (16 figures: main, appendix, and supplement).
evidence_items.title: CMIP6 biogeochemical models under-represent the deep chlorophyll maximum and diverge in how they express it: a regime-based BGC-Argo evaluation in the North Pacific — data and code

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.
evidence_items.title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging

evidence_items.summary: Code, codebook, anonymised coding data and result tables for the article “Sludge in Digital Finance: Evidence from 93,000 User Reviews of Chilean Banking and FinTech Apps”. The study analyses 93,243 Google Play reviews (2023–2026) of five incumbent banks and two neobanks/digital wallets in Chile, combining a structural topic model with the manual coding of a stratified sample of 1,400 reviews (two independent coders, one of them a large language model, plus a second human coder on a 210-review subsample). Review texts are not redistributed, to respect Google Play’s terms of service and users’ privacy; reviews are identified by a truncated SHA-256 hash that the collection script reproduces. Version 3 adds robustness checks, full-corpus topic–rating models, time trends of friction topics and analyses of developer replies (Tables 5–6, Figure 3).
evidence_items.title: Replication package — Sludge in Digital Finance: Evidence from 93,000 User Reviews of Chilean Banking and FinTech Apps
