evidence_items.summary: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.
evidence_items.title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors

evidence_items.summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.
evidence_items.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a 3 times 3 factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across 12 representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to 64%), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.
evidence_items.title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?

evidence_items.summary: Objective Negative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institution's data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. Methods Four LLM agents operate on an institution's Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospital's electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. Results MENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was κ=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. Conclusion Combining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone.
evidence_items.title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes

evidence_items.summary: The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) for code generation is reshaping how programming is practiced in educational contexts. Rather than treating this shift as a replacement for traditional programming instruction, this poster frames ''vibe coding'' as a pedagogical design space in which students learn to specify, interrogate, and validate AI-generated code. Drawing on recent work in computing education and curriculum guidance on generative AI integration, we propose a structured set of classroom activities that reposition students as evaluators and refiners of model outputs rather than solely implementers of algorithms. The design space is informed by research on LLM-supported programming education, curriculum integration efforts, and known risks such as hallucinated or insecure code generation. We outline three activity types: prompt refinement tasks, multi-model comparison exercises, and failure analysis of generated code. We further propose initial evaluation dimensions for future empirical study, including specification quality, debugging reasoning, and evaluative judgement of generated artefacts.
evidence_items.title: Vibe Coding as a Pedagogical Design Space Within Programming Education

evidence_items.summary: Educators increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as student models: to summarize a learner's work, describe their understanding, and predict their next moves. For educators evaluating these tools, a fragile assumption sits underneath: a model's response can sound tailored to a student while only reflecting the programming situation. We ask whether an LLM's descriptions and predictions about novice Python programmers are tied to the specific student. We study introductory Python submissions from CodeBench, using 117 narrative cases and a matched-peer prediction audit of 310 paired comparisons. Written summaries appear personalized at the surface level: varied, behaviorally grounded, with little template language. A stricter prediction test reveals a gap. For students matched on the same exercise assessment state, predictions without process traces are roughly twice as similar in predicted activity shape (local run-count agreement) as students' real next submissions, while other granularities show smaller or uncertain effects. Adding traces reduces this collapse and adds coarse repair-magnitude and structural signal, but reliable trace-added gains for code details, edit locations, or identifiers remain absent. For educators evaluating LLM-powered tools, personalized-sounding summaries are insufficient evidence of student-specific modeling. We propose identity perturbation under matched assessment state: pair students at the same exercise and test-outcome state, then test whether predictions are correctly targeted, not merely varied. Personalization claims should specify what student-specific signal is captured, from coarse behavior to fine-grained code, so educators and tool designers can judge when LLM-based personalization is warranted.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM Student Models Track the Student or the Situation? A Matched-Peer Study in Novice Programming

evidence_items.summary: Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) are attractive as educational tutors because they can keep student data inside the institution, yet they must read untrusted student input, which exposes them to prompt injection. In practice, the most troubling attacks may not be the most obvious ones. A teacher or platform reviewer can notice a message that says ''ignore all previous instructions.'' It is much harder to notice an instruction hidden in Base64, buried in a code comment, framed as ordinary help-seeking, or placed in a document-ingestion channel such as PDF metadata or annotations. As a secondary analysis of an anonymized educational prompt-injection benchmark, this poster regroups the attacks by expected detectability : whether an attack is likely to be noticed during routine educational review. Across 37 adversarial prompts and ten runs per model, Llama~3.2~3B is more vulnerable to hard-to-notice attacks than to obvious ones (50.0% strict Attack Success Rate (ASR) versus 27.9%). The opaque subset---encoded and document-ingestion payloads---reaches 44.5% ASR. Phi-3-mini shows lower confirmed attack success, but mostly because many responses drift off topic or become unusable rather than safely refusing. The pedagogical lesson is that a tutor that mishandles hard-to-notice attacks can give students inappropriate help, leak protected instructions, or produce unreliable feedback while still appearing safe under a simple success-rate metric. We argue that human reviewability should be designed, measured, and protected as part of AI-supported teaching.
evidence_items.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: When Hard-to-Notice Prompt Injections Undermine Educational SLM Tutors

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in programming courses to generate code, explain concepts, and support debugging. In pair programming, their use creates a new form of collaboration in which students must coordinate not only with one another but also with an AI system. Although pair programming is widely adopted in computing education, instructors often have limited visibility into how students divide work, negotiate solutions, and develop shared understanding, particularly when generative AI tools are involved. Existing evaluations typically emphasize final code quality, grades, or students' perceptions, offering limited insight into how dialogue, programming actions, and LLM use interact and evolve over time. This paper presents a multimodal framework for studying semester-long LLM-supported pair programming in undergraduate programming courses. The framework integrates three data sources: video-based dialogue transcripts, programming activity logs, and LLM interaction logs. Dialogue and LLM exchanges are qualitatively coded, while programming logs are converted into labeled action sequences. Sequence pattern mining is then used to identify recurring collaboration, programming, and LLM-use trajectories. Cross-modal analysis examines how these trajectories align at the week and semester levels, and how the resulting patterns relate to course grades and other available learning outcomes. By making these interaction processes more visible, the study aims to identify recurring patterns of LLM-supported collaboration and generate evidence for instructors that can inform the design of pair-programming activities.
evidence_items.title: Toward Understanding Collaboration and Learning in LLM-Supported Pair Programming

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT)-oriented lesson planning in a preservice teacher education context, examining the extent to which LLM use can contribute to the mobilisation of TBLT-related competencies. The case study draws on triangulated data from surveys, interaction logs with the LLM, lesson plans produced by preservice teachers and their reflections. The module required participants to generate a lesson plan with an LLM and to compare the resulting plan with a previously created lesson plan developed without AI support. The analysis focuses on knowledge of TBLT principles and their implementation during lesson planning, and the GenAI competence activated through the interaction with the LLM. The findings reveal considerable variation in how the dyads interacted with the LLM. Some dyads formulated more precise prompts and prompt iterations, provided more contextualised input, engaged more critically with the LLM-generated output, and iteratively refined their lesson plans in ways that appeared more consistent with TBLT principles. The data suggest an association between a stronger conceptual understanding of TBLT and more purposeful interaction with the LLM. This association indicates that disciplinary knowledge may facilitate the effective use of LLMs for TBLT-oriented lesson planning. Rather than replacing pedagogical expertise, LLM use appears to be most productive when preservice teachers are able to critically evaluate and adapt the generated output in light of established TBLT principles.
evidence_items.title: Generative AI Literacies and Discipline-Specific Knowledge: Preservice Teachers Planning Task-Based L2 Lessons with GenAI

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming computer science (CS) education by providing immediate problem solving support and on-demand knowledge. However, commercial LLMs frequently deliver complete solutions, fostering overreliance and diminishing the productive struggle essential for deep learning. Neurological evidence further suggests that LLM dependence can significantly reduce brain activity, threatening long-term retention. In response, educators have begun customizing LLM-based AI assistants to deliver structured scaffolding. Despite these efforts, the effect of cognitive offloading in student–AI interactions on CS learning outcomes remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Chat-Bloom (CB), a taxonomy that classifies the cognitive offloading level of both student prompts and AI responses. We validated CB through inter-rater reliability testing (Gwet's AC2 = 0.81) and trained machine learning (ML) models to achieve 81% classification accuracy for large-scale analysis. Applying CB to CS1 chat logs, we identify distinct interaction sequences, compare cognitive offloading patterns across AI assistants, and examine their relationship to student outcomes. These findings position CB as a practical framework for evaluating and improving AI-assisted learning in CS education.
evidence_items.title: Chat-Bloom: A Taxonomy for Classifying Cognitive Offloading in Student-AI Interactions in CS Education

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) for code generation is transforming software development and necessitating a rethinking of how programming should be taught. Although AI can often produce syntactically and functionally correct code, such code is not necessarily of high quality; humans must still evaluate it for qualities such as readability, maintainability, modularity, and design. Yet introductory computing curricula often emphasize functional correctness, while code quality topics such as decomposition, modularity, and design, are postponed until upper-level software development courses. As a result, students may have little opportunity to develop the habits and vocabulary needed to assess code structure and make informed design choices. This gap is increasingly consequential as students rely on AI tools that can produce working code without making their design tradeoffs visible. We argue that introductory programming courses should teach code quality alongside functional correctness, particularly in the age of AI. From the beginning of the curriculum, students should learn why code quality matters, how to evaluate both human- and AI-generated code, and how to write programs that are not only correct but also readable, maintainable, and well designed.
evidence_items.title: The Growing Importance of Code Quality Instruction in the AI Era

evidence_items.summary: K-12 students often struggle with foundational programming concepts such as variables, data types, loops, and conditionals. Large language models (LLMs) can provide immediate help, but unconstrained AI support may act as an answer engine, revealing solutions and reducing productive struggle. This work presents an exploratory design and feasibility evaluation of answer-aware LLM hints for an interactive K-12 programming platform. The system receives structured problem context, including the correct answer as private information, and is prompted to generate progressive hints that guide reasoning without directly revealing the solution. The design is motivated by two needs: reducing the authoring burden of manually writing multiple hints for each programming question, and adding guardrails so generated hints remain age-appropriate, context-aligned, and non-revealing. We evaluated the system using post-activity surveys from 46 students ages 7-11 and 4 STEM instructors, along with automated hint-quality metrics and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Students and instructors generally perceived the hints as useful, confidence-supporting, and preferable to direct answer display. Automated evaluation suggested that generated hints were usually grounded in the activity context while avoiding excessive reference to the correct answer.
evidence_items.title: Answer-Aware LLM Hints to Scaffold Deeper Learning in K-12 Programming Education

evidence_items.summary: As computer science (CS) education evolves, emerging technologies — including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), gamification, and mobile learning — are increas- ingly reshaping instructional practices and learning environments. This systematic literature review synthesizes empirical findings from 75 peer-reviewed studies to critically evaluate the pedagogi- cal value, effectiveness, and implementation challenges associated with integrating these technologies into CS classrooms. Drawing on thematic analysis across five research questions, this review examines how immersive environments foster deeper conceptual understanding, how AI-driven tutoring systems enable adaptive and personalized learning experiences, and how game-based and mobile learning tools enhance student engagement and intrinsic motivation. Key themes emerging from the literature include the benefits of interactivity, accessibility, and learner-centered per- sonalization, alongside persistent barriers such as infrastructural limitations, cost constraints, and insufficient instructor professional development. The review further highlights how blended learning models and social technologies support flexible, student-centered pedagogical approaches, while identifying critical gaps in longitu- dinal evidence, standardized assessment frameworks, and equitable access across diverse learner populations. To address these gaps, this paper presents a structured set of future research directions spanning longitudinal effectiveness, K–12 applications, inclusive design, ethical governance, and the emerging convergence of im- mersive environments with large language models. The insights offered are intended to inform educators, researchers, and policy- makers seeking to advance evidence-based, scalable, and inclusive technology integration in CS education.
evidence_items.title: Immersive and Interactive Technologies in Computer Science Education: A Systematic Review
Deep learning for learning outcome prediction and evaluation in Wushu physical education

evidence_items.summary: As higher education institutions increasingly adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support curriculum mapping, these pipelines rely heavily on text embedding models to align internal module/course learning outcomes (LO) with degree programme outcomes and external accreditation standards. However, a critical assumption remains largely untested: do general-purpose text embedding models used to compare LO similarity adequately represent the unique, multidimensional semantics of pedagogical texts? In educational theory, an LO is not an ordinary sentence; it strictly binds a disciplinary topic to a specific cognitive process (e.g., Bloom's Taxonomy). General-purpose models risk conflating these orthogonal dimensions, prioritising topical overlap while ignoring pedagogical rigor. Using a dataset of 6,790 authentic LOs from a UK higher education institution, this work investigates whether current text embedding models capture this bipartite structure in their vector embeddings. Through a controlled semantic perturbation methodology: comparing verb ablation against cognitive tier changing, we quantify how vector spaces distort pedagogical intent when distinct cognitive actions share identical subject matter. Preliminary findings indicate that standard embedding models are overwhelmingly dominated by topical context, effectively rendering cognitive verbs invisible in the latent space. This systematic fusion poses severe false-positive risks for automated curriculum auditing, highlighting the need for pedagogy-aware text embeddings.
evidence_items.title: Can Text Embeddings Distinguish Cognitive Depth in Learning Outcomes?

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the technology labor market and raising fundamental questions regarding the adequacy of traditional Computing Undergraduate Programs (CUPs) in preparing graduates for evolving software development practices. Historically, entry level software development roles have served as a critical transition between academic study and professional practice. However, the increasing integration of GenAI-based tools automates routine coding tasks, thereby reducing the relative importance of basic programming. At the same time, it elevates the need for higher-order competencies, including system level reasoning, architectural design, system integration, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, as well as concerns of security and reliability. Correspondingly, graduates face increasing difficulty in securing initial positions. These developments raise the question of whether existing CUP structures provide an adequate foundation for early-career competencies. In response, this spotlight proposes a staged modular structure organized into coherent packs, each pack includes courses, defined learning outcomes and competences alongside integrative projects. In addition, the proposed modular structure identifies the appropriate point, recognized by the institutions that will grant professional certificates, with which students can begin engaging in entry-level professional roles while continuing their academic studies. Such parallel engagement may create a feedback loop between academic learning and professional practice: practical experience can deepen the relevance and value of academic study, while continued coursework can support more reflective, informed, and theoretically grounded professional development.
evidence_items.title: Toward Industry-Aligned, Flexible, Computing Undergraduate Programs in the AI Era

evidence_items.summary: In today's technology-driven world, data and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is critical across all different job sectors. While curricula in science and engineering disciplines are updated routinely to reflect the need for data and AI literacy, this is not the case for liberal arts disciplines. In fact, coursework within most liberal arts disciplines does not explicitly emphasize improving students' data and AI literacy. In this work, we use occupational-skill data and domain-expert interpretation to identify potential data and AI literacy gaps in selected liberal arts curricula. Our study finds that current LA coursework provides limited explicit training in the data and AI literacy skills demanded by many LA-oriented careers. We also describe how integrating data and AI literacy projects into existing coursework can support students' development of these skills and present preliminary evidence of promise from a mixed formative evaluation across four projects.
evidence_items.title: Improving Data and AI Literacy in Liberal Arts Curriculum: A Project-based Approach

evidence_items.summary: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in programming education has intensified concerns about the transparency and reproducibility of empirical studies involving code generation, automated feedback, and AI-assisted tutoring. Existing research frequently underreports critical methodological details such as prompt design, development environments, evaluation protocols, and mechanisms for validating AI-generated code, limiting interpretability and replication. While the Reporting AI Studies in Education (RAISE) framework provides a comprehensive structure for improving reporting quality, its generic educational wording does not consistently specify the technical and methodological details required for programming education studies, where executable artefacts, development toolchains, and debugging processes are central to study design. This paper proposes RAISE-Prog, a domain-specific extension of RAISE for AI-supported programming education studies. It retains RAISE's ten-domain, thirty-item structure while adapting and extending individual reporting requirements, including reproducible coding environments, prompt and workflow specification, code validation practices, and academic integrity considerations in AI-assisted programming tasks. The paper outlines the rationale for the extension, presents the adapted checklist, and discusses directions for future validation through community consensus and empirical evaluation.
evidence_items.title: RAISE-Prog: Extending the Reporting AI Studies in Education Framework for Programming Education

organizations: Nova Southeastern University, Fort Lauderdale, FL, USA
evidence_items.summary: Computing students experience challenges with negative perceptions toward writing and communicating technical ideas. While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) writing tools provide immediate support, they often generate complete written content, which may reduce students' active participation and sense of ownership. ProseSpark is introduced as a consent-based agentic AI writing companion designed to support computing students without writing on their behalf. ProseSpark is grounded in human-centered AI and self-regulated learning theory to maintain student autonomy and encourage active engagement throughout the writing process. This poster presents ProseSpark's design principles, platform, and responsible-AI safeguards. Future evaluation will examine how workflow-oriented AI support influences computing students' motivation, engagement, and writing self-efficacy.
evidence_items.title: ProseSpark: Preserving Student Agency in Computing Writing with an Agentic AI Companion

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to computing education, yet its environmental implications are largely absent from curricula. While students learn to optimise predictive performance, efficiency, and correctness, the energy consumption and carbon footprint of AI systems remain peripheral concerns. This omission risks normalising unsustainable practices among future computing professionals. We introduce the Sustainable Computing in AI (SCAI) framework, a structured approach for embedding environmental responsibility into AI education. SCAI integrates three interrelated layers: (1) the Lifecycle Layer, which identifies environmental impact across data, training and fine-tuning, deployment and inference, and maintenance stages; (2) the Evaluation Layer, which extends traditional performance metrics to incorporate energy, computational efficiency, and model appropriateness; and (3) the Pedagogical Layer, which specifies learning outcomes, instructional activities, and assessment strategies that foreground sustainability. By connecting technical decision-making, assessment, and pedagogy, SCAI transforms sustainability from an abstract principle into an explicit, assessable component of coursework.
evidence_items.title: Sustainable Computing in AI (SCAI) Framework: Integrating Environmental Responsibility into AI Education

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more prevalent in daily life, developing AI literacy and computational thinking (CT) in K--12 students is increasingly important. Recent AI education programs focus heavily on machine learning (ML), but rule-based systems lie at the intersection of CT and symbolic AI, offering an opportunity to teach both. The recent interest in neuro-symbolic AI highlights the continued relevance of symbolic reasoning. To address this need, we developed RuleRunners, a novel web application that teaches rule-based systems through a gamified parkour environment. In this work, our research questions were: (RQ1) How does RuleRunners impact student learning of rule-based systems?; (RQ2) How do students compare rule-based systems and machine learning models?; and (RQ3) How engaging is the two-player collaborative and competitive design of RuleRunners? We evaluated RuleRunners at an in-classroom AI Expo event with 8th grade students, collecting qualitative and quantitative data to assess student learning and engagement. Our results show that RuleRunners effectively helped students understand the fundamentals of rule-based systems and some advantages over ML models. Furthermore, we found that interaction with RuleRunners led to a statistically significant improvement in performance on a matched pre- and post-survey item about rules. These findings suggest that RuleRunners can be adopted to support K--12 AI education initiatives, as it fosters AI literacy and CT through a collaborative, engaging experience.
evidence_items.title: RuleRunners: A Two-Player Collaborative Software Tool for Introducing Rule-Based AI Systems to Middle School Students

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence is developing at a rapid pace resulting in rising concerns relating to the ethical implications of this technology. AI professionals are in greater demand alongside a concomitant increase in interest in studying this topic. AI educational programs primarily teach the technical components of this domain, with ethical and socio-technical concerns seen as an optional extra. Therefore, a change in pedagogical approach is imperative to ensure the future AI workforce are critical and socially responsible practitioners. We propose a critical pedagogical methodology to interweave intersectionality, ethics and social responsibility into AI education to address the inequalities of AI in society. Tangible approaches to a critical AI curriculum are outlined in this paper including incorporating algorithmic social impact assessments, datasheets for datasets and embedding ethics within technical assessment to demonstrate to students the intrinsic socio-technical nature of AI.
evidence_items.title: CAP: Critical AI Pedagogy

evidence_items.summary: To investigate local erosion in split-frame aqueducts under sediment-laden flow, a three-dimensional water–sediment two-phase numerical model was developed using the RNG k–ε turbulence model, the Discrete Phase Model (DPM), and the Neilson–Gilchrist erosion model. The model was validated against flume-test data for pier erosion. The effects of discharge, sediment concentration, and particle size on erosion at different aqueduct sections were then examined, and pier-end aspect-ratio schemes were compared in terms of velocity distribution and erosion response. The mean relative error between simulated and measured erosion thicknesses under four benchmark inlet velocities was 6.76%. The inlet split-frame pier region, upstream aqueduct body, and turning zones of the outlet transition section were identified as the main high-erosion regions. Within the tested range, erosion generally increased with discharge, sediment concentration, and particle size. A combined scheme with AR₁ = 1.5 at the inlet and AR₂ = 2.0 at the outlet produced a smoother velocity transition, reduced the outlet wake-affected region, and yielded lower model-predicted erosion rates than the original semi-circular configuration in most cases. These results provide numerical support for erosion-risk identification and preliminary pier-geometry selection in similar water-conveyance structures.
evidence_items.title: Numerical simulation of water-sediment two-phase erosion in a split-frame aqueduct and comparison of pier geometry schemes
Environmental Impact of Cataract Surgery Packs: Benchmarking Real-World Practice Through the ESCRS SIDICS Platform.
Qualifying AI software quality evaluators: a measurement systems analysis protocol for LLM code review and automated quality gates

evidence_items.summary: AI coding assistants have moved from autocomplete to agents that generate, run, and revise whole programs. As a result, software is increasingly being built by stating intent rather than writing code by hand. Furthermore, students are using these tools in their coursework. In an introductory course, 84 percent of students stated they used ChatGPT for their assignments, exposing a gap in assessment when these tools are at play. When an LLM writes the code, passing test suites alone does not show how well the student works with AI, because there are other expertise-revealing aspects of software development, like security. What separates a strong student (when AI is permitted) is how well they specify a task, direct an agent, and catch bad output. We present a competency framework that scores AI-assisted programming work along five competencies (problem solving, planning, prompting, verification, and agentic workflow) with an assessment design that offers three levels of AI availability. The framework runs in an online assessment platform we built and operate, and it reports interpretable results for each competency backed by evidence, though it is in early development and not yet widely used or validated. We describe the framework and its rationale while outlining a planned evaluation.
evidence_items.title: A Competency Framework for Assessing AI-Assisted Programming Work

evidence_items.summary: For decades, computing instructors have given students a specification, asked them to translate it into code, and evaluated the result against the specification. Coding agents can now complete most of these assessments with only a small number of prompts. Students who use AI this way learn neither what the assessment was meant to teach nor how to collaborate with AI effectively. Meanwhile, the rapid adoption of coding agents by developers is reshaping how technology is created. Working with them multiplies individual productivity, accelerates teams, and expands what computing can build. Agentic development is an important new skill. Students must learn it. Updated assessments are needed to teach it. This working group will map how computing educators are responding. In July 2026, we organized a public workshop convening computing educators to discuss how they intended to redesign assessments in response to AI and prepared a public report from those discussions. Then, we will survey computing educators to identify assessments that have been redesigned, replaced, or deliberately preserved, along with the rationale behind each choice. Finally, we will assemble what we discover into a taxonomy that can help future computing education researchers and practitioners design assessments that resist AI delegation and assessments that teach students to direct it.
evidence_items.title: AI Can Do Your Homework. Now What-: Developing a Taxonomy of Computing Assessments That Accommodate GenAI Use

evidence_items.summary: Vibecoding, building software by stating intent to an AI in natural language instead of hand-coding it, is spreading quickly through industry and entrepreneurship. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 84% of developers reported using or planning to use AI coding tools, and Y Combinator, a startup accelerator, disclosed in early 2025 that a quarter of its most recent startup batch participants had codebases that were roughly 95% AI-generated. As the workforce moves in this direction, graduates need skills that conventional curricula, still built around writing code by hand, seldom teach directly, such as writing precise specifications, supervising AI coding agents, and verifying code that looks plausible but may be wrong or insecure. In a 2024 Cengage survey, 70% of recent graduates said training in generative AI should be integrated into coursework. We present Vibecoding: Introduction to Applied AI, an openly licensed curriculum, released early and still under active development. It comprises a textbook, lecture slides, a syllabus, and a hands-on lab for every chapter. The coursework runs from specification writing through building full-stack applications to critically evaluating AI-generated output. It is sequenced in this way so that students build competence with AI tools before confronting the shortcomings and limitations of such tools. We describe the curriculum's design and rationale while outlining our plan to pilot and evaluate it in the classroom.
evidence_items.title: Teaching Vibecoding: An Open Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Development

evidence_items.summary: Learning resource recommendation is an important component of intelligent educational systems. Most existing approaches rely on students' online learning traces, such as historical responses and interaction logs, while the rich learning signals from face-to-face classroom instruction remain underutilized. In this paper, we propose an engagement-aware exercise recommendation system that explicitly integrates offline classroom engagement with knowledge-based similarity modeling. The proposed system estimates time-varying collective engagement from students' head pose data, segments lecture recordings into instructional units, and extracts structured knowledge components from both lecture content and candidate exercises through a multi-agent collaborative framework powered by large multimodal models. By aligning engagement scores temporally with lecture segments, the system assigns greater weight to instructional content associated with lower engagement and prioritizes semantically aligned exercises to provide additional learning support for these segments. The effectiveness of the proposed system is evaluated through simulation-based recommendation experiments using data collected from an undergraduate Computer Organization course taught in a blended learning setting. Our results demonstrate that our system leads to higher predicted knowledge states, with an average relative increase of 15.4%, and confirm that the engagement-aware weighting mechanism contributes to this simulated improvement.
evidence_items.title: Engagement-Aware Exercise Recommendation System Based on Multimodal Analysis for Blended Learning
Lexico-syntactic complexity in human and AI-generated outputs across interpreting and translation: a paired-corpus study

evidence_items.summary: Open-source GitHub Action that reviews pull requests with NVIDIA Nemotron on Nebius Token Factory. Pre-registered benchmarks; every loss published.
evidence_items.title: SunnyBagal/TraceHound

evidence_items.summary: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
evidence_items.title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence

evidence_items.summary: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for surgical quality assessment promise to democratize access to expertise, with applications in training, guidance, and accreditation. This study presents the SAGES Critical View of Safety (CVS) Challenge, the first AI competition organized by a surgical society, using the CVS in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a universally recommended yet inconsistently performed safety step, as an exemplar of surgical quality assessment. A global collaboration across 54 institutions in 24 countries engaged hundreds of clinicians and engineers to curate 1,000 videos annotated by 20 surgical experts according to a consensus-validated protocol. The challenge addressed key barriers to real-world deployment in surgery, including achieving high performance, capturing uncertainty in subjective assessment, and ensuring robustness to clinical variability. To enable this scale of effort, we developed EndoGlacier, a framework for managing large, heterogeneous surgical video and multi-annotator workflows. Thirteen international teams participated, achieving up to a 17% relative gain in assessment performance, over 62% reduction in calibration error, and a 17% relative improvement in robustness over the state-of-the-art. Analysis of results highlighted methodological trends linked to model performance, providing guidance for future research toward robust, clinically deployable AI for surgical quality assessment.
evidence_items.title: The SAGES Critical View of Safety Challenge: A Global Benchmark for AI-Assisted Surgical Quality Assessment

evidence_items.summary: A Spring Boot backend service for the AI DIAL Admin Evaluation Framework. This service manages the lifecycle of LLM/AI model evaluations, including test suite authoring, execution tracking, and metrics collection.
evidence_items.title: epam/ai-dial-admin-evaluation-framework-backend

evidence_items.summary: A harness-agnostic verification gate for multi-agent collaboration: spec + gate CLI + card linter, signed off by four independent review rounds.
evidence_items.title: 91-5/agent-covenant

evidence_items.summary: Local first AI evaluation engine
evidence_items.title: BraveRam/evalgate

evidence_items.title: ishtiaqrahman/capitalbench

organizations: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro
Instituto de Estudos do Mar Almirante Paulo Moreira
evidence_items.summary: Tropical reefs are among the most biodiverse and threatened marine ecosystems and face both local and global stressors. Understanding community dynamics and ecosystem functioning under these pressures requires long-term monitoring. Image-based surveys are increasingly used in reef ecology because they enable rapid data acquisition and storage. However, manual identification of benthic organisms is time-consuming and potentially subjective, creating a bottleneck between image collection and ecological analysis. Automated annotation tools represent promising solutions, but few studies have directly compared their performance with that of manual approaches, especially under varying image quality conditions. Here, we assess the usefulness of the CoralNet automated tool for classifying benthic cover in tropical reef images and evaluate how image quality influences both manual and automated annotations. Using expert-validated images, we trained and tested both approaches, measuring performance with Cohen’s Kappa coefficient and modeling the effects of image imperfections. We found that manual and automated annotators achieved similar performance across most taxonomic and morphofunctional groups, and both were similarly affected by image quality. Importantly, although the automated annotator showed a slightly lower performance than the manual annotator, image-quality imperfections had a stronger influence on annotation performance than annotator type itself. Our findings indicate that automated annotation can provide comparable performance to manual methods once appropriately trained, with strong potential to enhance large-scale monitoring, biodiversity assessments, and conservation strategies in reef ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Humans versus machines: artificial intelligence performs similarly to manual analysis in benthic reef monitoring
